+ Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 76.3
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
Arthur Neegan adjusted his collar for the seventh time since the transfer vessel had left Mars. The collar was too high. It belonged to a charcoal suit delivered to his house that morning in a sealed diplomatic case, along with a note asking him to dress for a formal meeting. The note had said nothing about the six armed people who would arrive an hour later. Through the port, Mars had dwindled to a red disk. Its night side was pricked with settlement lights and the blue sparks of ore ships climbing from the mines. “Is the suit uncomfortable, Mr. Neegan?” asked the woman opposite him. “It’s comfortable enough everywhere but the neck.” “I’ll inform the supplier.” “I’d rather you told me where we’re going.” The woman wore the dark uniform of the Antares Diplomatic Corps. Its insignia—a silver star between two outstretched hands—was embroidered above her heart. Arthur had seen the same mark on the transport that settled labour disputes at gunpoint in the southern mines. “We’re docking at Port Authority Station,” she said. “That’s a destination. Who am I meeting?” “I haven’t been authorised to say.” Arthur pulled at his collar. “Who authorised the rifles at my house?” “You were free to refuse transport.” “And stay there with your people guarding my doors?” She accepted this without embarrassment. “You were free to remain in your house.” The vessel’s engine gave a soft click as it shut down. For an instant Arthur felt weightless, and his stomach rose toward the troublesome collar. His plot lay west of the great corporate leases, on land his parents had claimed when land on Mars was still thought useful chiefly for keeping people employed. He had spent twenty years making its thin soil productive and its rock foundations stable. He knew precisely where to put a support beneath a tunnel and how long a pressure seal would last in dust. He had never learned how to protect a house from discovery. Three days earlier, his drill had cut a seam of Azra wider than his hand. The survey crew had traced it downward until their instruments failed. The woman saw him looking at the planet. “Your home will be secure,” she said. “That sounds like something you tell a man you don’t intend to send home.” “It’s something I can tell you because I’ve seen the orders.” The meeting room had a round table, four chairs, and a window facing away from Mars. Antares hung in that direction, too far away to distinguish from the other stars. An older man waited at the table. He stood when Arthur entered. “Councillor Pell,” the man said. “Please sit.” Arthur remained standing. “Which council?” “The Interplanetary Commission on Strategic Materials.” “I’ve never heard of it.” “Until last week, it had three members and a filing cabinet.” Pell gestured at the chair. “Now it has seventeen members and a battleship.” Arthur sat. The woman from the vessel took a place by the door. Pell touched a control in the table, and a map of Arthur’s claim appeared between them in pale green light. A red line marked the vein. “That line is wrong,” Arthur said. “It runs beneath the house.” Pell studied the map. “You’re certain?” “I installed the house’s foundations. Your surveyor started his measurements forty metres too far south.” Pell made a note. “That may change the construction schedule.” “What construction schedule?” “We’ll come to it. First, I’d like to know what you’ve been told about Azra.” “It makes radioactive material decay faster. That makes it valuable for drives, and valuable to anyone who wants a weapon to deliver more energy than its fuel ought to.” “A fair summary. It also makes waste stores less permanent, if we can learn to control it. On most worlds, an Azra deposit can be measured in kilograms. Yours may contain thousands of tonnes.” Arthur looked again at the red line. His house was a small square on the map. “The corporations know,” he said. “They know enough. Two have filed claims against your survey. A third has discovered that your father’s original settlement grant was issued on a day when the registry clock was eleven minutes slow.” “Does that matter?” “It matters to someone willing to pay a judge.” Pell dismissed the map and opened a document in its place. “The Commission proposes to purchase your mineral rights. You will receive payment at the highest valuation submitted by any claimant. Your land and home remain yours, subject to an easement for a research installation.” “An installation beneath my house.” “Possibly.” “Then I decline.” Pell folded his hands. “I expected you might. May I explain why I asked you here before you decide?” Arthur glanced toward the woman at the door. “I seem to have time.” “Each corporation believes that if another learns to refine Azra first, its own fleet becomes obsolete. The Antares government believes the same of every government closer to Mars. Your vein is large enough to settle that competition for a generation—or start a war over it next month.” “And this Commission will keep everybody honest?” “No. We’re attempting to give them a reason to remain patient.” Pell enlarged a paragraph of the document. Arthur read it twice. “You want my help appointing the labour overseer?” “I want you to be the labour overseer.” “I’m an engineer.” “Which is why I’d prefer you to a lawyer. The corporations will supply workers under the lease system. The Commission can inspect the work, but inspections announced from orbit see very little. We need someone at the site who understands what a safe shaft looks like.” Arthur thought of the workers he had seen waiting outside lease offices, carrying their possessions in numbered cases. A mine could be made safe. It could also be made cheap. “What authority would I have?” “To close a shaft. To stop work on a machine. To hear complaints in private.” “And if I close a shaft they want open?” “Your order stands until the Commission hears an appeal.” “That may be two weeks.” “Yes.” Arthur looked at him. “You’ve offered me a way to make enemies.” “You already have them. I’m offering you work worth doing while they decide what to do about you.” The room remained quiet for a moment. A vessel crossed the window, black against the stars, its running lights pulsing red and white. “Why does the Antares Diplomatic Corps carry your invitations?” Arthur asked. Pell’s eyes moved briefly to the woman by the door. “Because its ships can pass the blockade,” he said. “What blockade?” “The one that will be announced tomorrow.” Arthur stood. “You might have led with that.” “I wanted you to read the terms first.” He reached for his collar again, then stopped. The suit was still uncomfortable; on that point, at least, nothing had changed. “I’ll read them,” Arthur said. “All of them. Then I want to speak to my lawyer and my neighbours.” Pell nodded. “There’s a communications room next door.” “Before that, correct your map. If you build where that red line says to build, you’ll break into the old water shaft.” Pell called the map back at once. Arthur leaned over the table and put his finger on the place where the first tunnel must go.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a competent pastiche of Asimov: restrained, dialogue-driven, with big-picture geopolitics delivered through conversation and small-picture detail (the collar, the surveyor's forty-metre error, the registry clock eleven minutes slow). The dialogue is crisp and functional, with the dry, chess-like negotiation feel Asimov favored. Pell is a plausible bureaucratic antagonist/ally, and the offer structure (mineral rights purchase, overseer role) is well-motivated. The blockade reveal is a good hook for larger intrigue. Arthur's characterization is consistent: an engineer who thinks in foundations and pressure seals, and who corrects the map at the end — a nice characterizing beat. Weaknesses: the prose is competent but flat in places; description is sparse (the prompt asked for vivid scene-setting interspersed, and there's relatively little); the emotional register is narrow — Arthur's fear/anger is understated to the point of blandness. Some exchanges (the collar) are effective; others are purely functional. The stakes are told more than felt. The ending is slightly neat. Still, it's coherent, purposeful, and stylistically faithful. + Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 60.9
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
By the third hour, the darkroom smelled like vinegar, wet paper, and the wool coat Elliot refused to take off. Under the red safelight, its black velvet collar looked almost purple. He had found it at a church rummage sale for eight dollars, which he’d told me with the private satisfaction other people reserved for getting into graduate school. I’d noticed him on the first day of experimental photography: lace-up boots, chipped silver nail polish, a thrift-shop nu-goth wardrobe assembled with more care than most gallery shows. Then he’d opened his mouth to ask our professor whether an image could still be called candid if the subject knew the photographer loved them. I’d spent the semester pretending that question hadn’t followed me home. Now we were partners for the final project, printing portraits of each other after campus had emptied out. “Ten seconds?” he asked, one hand hovering over the enlarger timer. “Eleven. I want the window to hold some detail.” He pressed the button. Light poured through my negative and onto the blank paper. In the photograph, I stood in the doorway of my apartment in a red suit, shoulders squared. Elliot had taken it the afternoon I told him to stop apologizing before every shot. Somehow he’d caught the moment after I said it, when I’d looked down and laughed. He slipped the paper into the developer. We watched my outline surface. “There you are,” he said. I was used to people saying things like that when they meant the suit. Elliot was looking at my face. My phone buzzed silently in my pocket. I left it there. For the next print, I chose a frame of him sitting on the floor beneath the studio’s north window. His coat fell open over a mesh shirt, and he held a dead moth between two careful fingers. In most of the roll, he looked directly at me. In this frame, his gaze was fixed on the moth. “I don’t know about that one,” he said. “We can print something else.” “No. I like it. It’s just…” He reached for the tongs, then set them down again. “You can see how hard I’m trying.” I had thought he looked calm. I looked back at the negative, suspended in its little plastic sleeve. “What were you trying to do?” He gave a short laugh. “Be the kind of person who wears this stuff without making it a whole thing.” “You’re allowed to make it a whole thing.” “That’s what I’m afraid of.” We ran a test strip. While it developed, he leaned against the counter, close enough that the sleeve of his coat brushed my arm. I could have stepped closer. Usually I would have. I liked being the one who made an invitation unmistakable. “Can I tell you something?” he asked. “Yes.” “I’ve been questioning my gender.” He watched the strip turn dark. “Not just what I wear. I don’t know where I’m going with it yet.” The ventilation fan rattled overhead. I wanted to say something perfect and immediate, something that would take the risk out of what he’d just done. I also wanted to ask him every question I had. Neither impulse seemed particularly useful to him. “Thank you for telling me,” I said. “Do you still want me to use he?” “For now, yeah.” He rubbed a thumb over a seam in his cuff. “I might try other pronouns sometime. I don’t want anyone deciding what that means before I do.” “Okay. You tell me.” He nodded, but kept worrying the seam. I picked up the test strip, checked the exposures, and handed it to him. He pointed to the fourth square. Our fingers touched when I turned the paper toward the light. In the red glow, he looked both younger and harder to read. He was nineteen; I was twenty-five. We were classmates, and I knew his own mind had nothing to do with my age, but I could hear myself slipping into the voice I used when I thought I knew the best way forward. I’d nearly offered to help him come out to people. He hadn’t said he wanted to come out at all. “We can use a different portrait,” I said. “Or shoot more. I don’t want the project to make you feel pinned down.” He looked at the test strip again. “I want to print this one. I just want to be the one who picks it.” “Then you pick it.” “I did.” He glanced up, smiling a little. “Fourth square.” I laughed and set the timer accordingly. As his image appeared in the tray, I found myself looking at him instead. I’d dated men with square-jawed confidence and women whose femininity filled a room before they entered it. I knew how to be attracted to what someone was certain of. With Elliot, what drew me closer was how seriously he paid attention to himself, even when he wasn’t sure what he’d find. I didn’t know what that said about me. I wasn’t ready to turn his questions into an answer to mine. He took the tongs and guided the print into the stop bath. “Is this weird?” he asked. “The picture?” “This. Telling you.” “I’m glad you did.” I paused. “And I’m attracted to you. I have been for a while.” His hand stopped above the tray. I wished, briefly, that I could pull the words back and give him more room around them. “You don’t have to say anything to that,” I added. “Especially not tonight.” “I was going to ask,” he said, “if you wanted to get coffee after we finish.” “Oh.” “And I’m glad you told me.” The print moved through the fixer. He lifted it for us to see: coat, moth, the light along his cheek. He had chosen the frame, and he seemed pleased with it now. “Coffee sounds good,” I said. “Good.” His smile widened. “Could we stay until the prints are washed, though?” “Absolutely.” He set the photograph in the wash tray beside mine. In the running water, the two sheets drifted apart, then bumped gently back together.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong, controlled piece of writing that fulfills nearly every requirement of the prompt with subtlety. The darkroom setting is used as more than backdrop—the red safelight, developer trays, test strips, and the ritual of printing become the structural spine of the scene, with the emerging photographs mirroring Elliot's gradual self-disclosure. The recurring motif of "choosing the frame" (Elliot insisting on picking the fourth square) elegantly embodies the theme of agency without stating it. Dani's voice is consistent and well-differentiated: assertive, wry, self-aware. Her internal conflict—wanting to take charge versus wanting to give Elliot room—is dramatized through concrete moments (nearly offering to help him come out, then catching herself; wishing she could pull back her confession) rather than explained. The dialogue is naturalistic and understated, with believable rhythms and a good ear for how people hedge around vulnerability ("Be the kind of person who wears this stuff without making it a whole thing"). The piece handles the gender-questioning content with unusual tact—no crisis, no lecture, no tidy resolution. Elliot remains somewhat opaque, which is appropriate to his POV-external position, though his characterization occasionally leans on the quirky-detail shorthand (dead moth, mesh shirt) that borders on the ornamental. The ending's image of the two prints drifting together in the wash is a touch sentimental but earned by the scene's restraint. The word count is somewhat under the 1000-word seed, though the seed reads as a target rather than a hard requirement. Minor weaknesses: the age-gap anxiety is raised and then somewhat waved away in a single sentence; the coffee-date resolution is slightly convenient; a few lines ("I wasn't ready to turn his questions into an answer to mine") flirt with the essayistic. But overall this is confident, mature work with genuine emotional complexity and no purple prose or overwrought moments. + Contemporary romance / drama: Stolen Moments in Roma — Score: 81.3
Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
Ben was halfway through a paragraph about the Trevi Fountain’s restoration when a motorcycle stopped so close to his knee that the corner of his guidebook folded in the wind. “Ma dove guardi?” the rider demanded. “Do you read while crossing the road in England too?” “I’m terribly sorry.” Ben stepped back onto the pavement. “I thought this was pedestrian— I mean, I didn’t see you.” “Excellent. We agree on one thing.” She lifted her visor. Dark eyes, a fierce mouth, a curl escaping her helmet. Behind her, the fountain’s roar filled the narrow street. Ben tried again. “Mi dispiace molto, signorina.” “Signorina?” Her expression changed. “How old is that book?” “Published last year.” “I meant the Italian inside your head.” He looked down at the mangled page, then back at her. She laughed, and despite the sweat cooling under his collar, he laughed too. Her phone buzzed on the handlebars. She glanced at it and swore. “I have a delivery.” “Of course. I’ve delayed you.” “You have.” She studied him for another second. “Where are you going?” Ben checked the page, although he knew. “The Pantheon.” “Then you’re going the wrong way.” “I was following a suggested route.” “This is Rome. The streets don’t follow suggested routes.” She lowered her visor and was gone. At the next corner, Ben found her waiting beside the motorcycle. She held out a spare helmet. “I have twenty minutes before anyone notices I’m late,” she said. “Are you coming?” *** Alessandra drove like someone conducting an argument with traffic and winning. Ben clung to the grab rail, reciting the names of emperors whenever they passed too close to a bus. At a red light, she turned her head. “You can hold on to me, professore. The motorcycle won’t be offended.” “I’m not a professor.” “You have elbow patches.” “It’s a linen jacket.” “Worse.” He put his hands carefully at her waist. When the light changed, she accelerated hard enough to make him tighten his grip. At a café near Largo Argentina, she delivered a padded envelope to a woman who called her a menace and kissed both her cheeks. Ben was still removing the helmet when Alessandra returned with two espressos. “You ordered for me?” “You looked as if you were about to ask whether they serve tea.” “I was about to ask for water.” She slid one cup towards him. “Even worse.” While he drank, she turned a little silver spoon between her fingers. The café woman called goodbye from inside. Alessandra’s hand went still; then the spoon vanished into her jacket pocket. Ben glanced up. She met his eyes without blinking. “So,” she said, “what do you study?” “Urban memory. How people understand a city through its monuments.” “People understand a city by trying to park in it.” He smiled. “That may be a stronger thesis.” *** By noon, his guidebook had disappeared into her motorcycle’s storage case. In Monti, she took him through a workshop courtyard where laundry hung above old stone basins. At the market in Testaccio, she made him order lunch. “Due supplì,” he told the vendor, then faltered. “Per favore.” “Beautiful,” Alessandra said. “Now ask what’s in them.” Ben looked at the row of golden croquettes. “Can’t I simply be surprised?” “That’s the spirit.” They ate standing up, molten cheese stretching between Ben’s fingers and his mouth. Alessandra watched him with unconcealed delight. “You have sauce on your face.” He searched his pockets for a handkerchief. She leaned in and wiped the corner of his mouth with her thumb. For a moment, the market noise receded. Then she held up her thumb. “Evidence.” “You could have told me where.” “I did.” Near the exit, she stopped at a rack of cheap postcards. Ben picked one showing the fountain at night. “Is this place always this crowded?” he asked. “The market? Only when you’re trying to get somewhere.” Outside, she took his guidebook from the storage case and tucked the postcard between its pages. He had not seen her pay. Before he could ask, she pointed across the road. “Come on. I’ll show you a quieter view.” *** On the Aventine Hill, Ben peered through the keyhole of the Knights of Malta gate and found St Peter’s perfectly framed in the distance. “Oh,” he said. Alessandra leaned against the wall, watching his face rather than the view. “Worth leaving the itinerary?” “It’s probably in the itinerary.” “Then I take it back.” Her phone rang. She let it ring out. A second later, it rang again. “Your delivery?” Ben asked. “My brother. He thinks because I work for myself, I can collect his dry cleaning.” “Can you?” “Yes. That isn’t the point.” He laughed. She checked the screen once more and put the phone away. For the first time all day, she seemed unsure what to do with her hands. “I should let you get back,” Ben said. “You should.” She pushed off the wall. “But we’re not near your hotel.” *** Clouds gathered as they crossed the river. Alessandra promised to return him to the centre, then took a turn towards Trastevere because, she said, he had not yet seen the street with the best laundry. Rain struck Ben’s visor in three large drops. By the time she parked, it was falling in sheets. They ran under the awning of a gelato shop, breathless and laughing. Water poured off its striped edge. Alessandra’s curls stuck to her forehead; Ben’s linen jacket had surrendered completely. “You’re a terrible guide,” he said. “I told you that this morning.” “No, you told me the streets were.” Through the shop window, a teenager stacked paper cups. Alessandra reached into her pocket and brought out the little silver spoon. She rolled it across her knuckles, then closed her fist around it. Ben looked at the spoon. “You could return it.” “To a café on the other side of the river?” “Tomorrow.” “Very British solution.” “I’ll come with you.” She turned towards him. Rain hissed against the pavement, hiding whatever passed across her face. “You’d cross Rome for a spoon?” Ben thought of his quiet flat in Bloomsbury, the notes waiting on his desk, the guidebook shut beneath her motorcycle seat. “I think,” he said, “I’ve crossed it for less today.” Alessandra slipped the spoon back into her pocket. Then she took his wet hand and pulled him into the gelato shop. “Tomorrow,” she said. “But first, you’re ordering.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of commercial romance writing. The prose is economical, witty, and confident, with sharp dialogue that carries most of the characterization. The opening near-collision is handled briskly and with humor; the banter ("Signorina? How old is that book?") lands well and establishes both voices immediately. The scene structure—Trevi, café, market, Aventine, Trastevere—gives the day a satisfying geographic and emotional arc. The kleptomania brief is handled with admirable subtlety: the silver spoon, the unpaid postcard, Ben noticing but not confronting, and the spoon becoming the emotional pivot of the ending. This is the piece's cleverest move—turning her compulsion into the pretext for a second meeting. The ambiguity of Alessandra's feelings is preserved; she remains enigmatic, and Ben's smitten disorientation is convincingly rendered through small details (reciting emperors' names, the surrendered linen jacket). Weaknesses: the piece is somewhat slight. The "wild, unsanctioned tour" never gets truly dangerous or outlandish—the riskiest thing is a motorcycle ride and a stolen spoon. The prompt asks for a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous moments; the delivery is gentler, more charming than thrilling. Some beats are familiar romance tropes (thumb-wiping sauce from the mouth, rain forcing them under an awning, the keyhole view on the Aventine). The brother/dry-cleaning phone call is a nice touch of interior life but is dropped rather than developed. Ben's transformation from polite academic to willing accomplice is incremental and plausible, though his "I've crossed it for less today" line gestures at depth the piece hasn't quite earned. The ending is warm but not saccharine, appropriately open. Dialogue is consistently the strongest element—fast, character-specific, never expository. Prose is clean, never purple. The piece is coherent, tight, and never meanders, though it arguably under-delivers on the prompt's demand for escalating outrageousness. + Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 82.5
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
At The Last Outpost, you can tell when the artificial gravity is about to hiccup by watching the drinks. The surface of a full glass draws itself into a little dome, as if taking a breath. “Five credits says it happens before Brin apologizes,” Lio says. Across the bar, Brin stares into her tea. “I said I was sorry.” “You said, ‘I’m sorry you took it that way.’” “That’s different from not apologizing.” “It certainly is.” The tea rises against one side of Brin’s cup. Every glass on the bar gives a soft, simultaneous clink. Then the gravity steadies. “Pay me,” Lio tells her. I slide a dish of warm salt biscuits between them. “Brin, tell Lio you shouldn’t have sold the engine parts he was saving. Lio, tell Brin you’re going to stop storing engine parts in the oven.” “It’s the only dry cupboard,” he says. “It’s an oven.” “An excellent dry cupboard.” The argument has been going on for three days. I expect it to last another two. That’s how most things work at the Outpost. Nobody has anywhere urgent to be, and being right is a pleasant way to pass the time. The door opens, and a stranger comes in from the docking corridor. Their tentacled dreads are askew, their travel coat hangs crooked, and they keep one hand pressed flat against an inner pocket. They sit at the end of my bar. “Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double.” I pour it. “Long trip?” “Not long enough.” They take a swallow and close their eyes. “Chased,” Brin murmurs, loudly enough for everyone to hear. The stranger opens one eye. “Is she always like that?” “Only with people,” I say. “I’m Nets.” They look at me for an uncomfortable beat. “Ivo Sen.” I know the name. Not Ivo’s, specifically. The Sen family keeps the old transit registers, the ones nobody consults unless something has gone wrong. “Your coat’s torn,” I say. “So is your station’s gravity.” “That’s a feature. Keeps the drinks lively.” Ivo’s mouth twitches. “Your jokes are worse than your gravity.” “They’re free with a double.” At the far table, Old Tam taps the wall screen, waiting for the evening ore prices. The screen stays dark. He taps it again. “No feed?” he calls. “Been patchy since noon,” I tell him. “It’s never patchy during a price drop.” Ivo sets down their glass. “That’s because a price drop isn’t what’s coming.” Lio leans an elbow on the bar. “What is?” Ivo glances at the door. “Do you have a private room?” “Upstairs,” I say. “Five credits an hour.” “For talking.” “Same price.” “Nets,” Brin says. “They look frightened.” “They also look like they can afford five credits.” Ivo puts a small metal case on the bar. Its seal carries the crest of Belt Survey. Underneath it, in lettering worn almost smooth, are the words *Original Anchor Assessment*. I stop smiling. Jo emerges from the kitchen with flour on her sleeves. Jo owns the Outpost, which means she is responsible for its air, its accounts, and the extraordinary number of people who come here to complain about both. “Why,” she asks Ivo, “do you have the assessment for my rock?” “Because somebody changed it.” Jo wipes her hands slowly. “Come upstairs.” Ivo doesn’t move. “It won’t help to keep this quiet. The survey tug is already on its way.” Tam gets up. “Survey tug? I’ve got a berth full of ore.” “Then you’ve got a problem,” Ivo says. Jo gives me a look. I know what it means: calm everyone down, and please don’t insult the person with the case. I can manage one of those. “Tea?” I ask Ivo. “Whisky.” “Tea first. Then you can tell us what changed.” I put the kettle on before they can answer. Its blue light comes on, goes off, then comes on again. Ivo notices. “How long has that been happening?” “Today,” Jo says. “Three weeks,” I say. Jo turns to me. “It was only flickering before today.” “You told me you fixed it.” “I told you I found the fault.” “Those aren’t the same thing, Nets.” “I’m aware of that now.” Ivo draws the case closer. “The Outpost’s anchor asteroid has a hollow seam. It was surveyed before the station was built. The original assessment forbids drilling within six hundred meters.” Brin straightens. “My crew’s new claim is four hundred meters from the station.” “The version your crew received says the seam is solid,” Ivo says. “A replacement survey went out last month.” “And Belt Survey let it through?” Jo asks. “No. Somebody used an old transit authorization to make it look as though it had always been there.” My fingers tighten around the kettle handle. I set it down. Lio sees. Lio always sees. “Nets?” “What authorization?” Ivo slides the case toward me. On its lid, a tiny reader wakes and displays a name I haven’t used in nine years. **NETTLE VALE — TRANSIT CONTROL.** Brin reads it aloud. “That’s you?” “Used to be.” “You worked for Transit?” Jo asks. “Briefly.” “Nine years isn’t briefly,” Ivo says. Nobody speaks. The gravity loosens for a breath, and the whisky in Ivo’s glass wobbles to the rim without spilling. Jo folds her arms. “Could Nets have changed the survey?” “No,” I say. Ivo looks at me. “Could someone use your authorization to do it?” “Yes.” “Why would it still be active?” “I don’t know.” I do know one reason it might be. When I left Transit, I walked out before the end of my shift and never went back to check what happened to my access. I can feel Jo waiting for me to say that. I can’t make myself do it in front of the room. Brin pushes away from the bar. “My crew starts drilling at first shift.” “You need to tell them not to,” Ivo says. “I will. And I want to see both surveys.” “You can.” The wall screen lights up at last. Tam turns toward it, relieved, but there are no ore prices. A docking request fills the display. **BELT SURVEY TUG *CROWN OF MOSS*. PRIORITY ACCESS REQUESTED.** Jo reads it once. “They’re early.” Ivo grips their glass. “Don’t give them the case.” Jo reaches for the intercom, then stops. “I haven’t decided what to give them.” On the screen, the request changes. **ACCESS CODE ACCEPTED. DOCKING CLAMPS ENGAGED.** “That’s not possible,” Jo says. “I didn’t authorize them.” I look down at the name glowing on the case. After nine years, I still remember my access code. Beyond the wall, something heavy locks into place.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of cozy sci-fi writing that hits nearly all the prompt requirements. The first-person present tense is maintained throughout, the dialogue ratio is comfortably around 60%, the conflict (the falsified survey, Nets's compromised transit authorization, the arriving tug) is established and left unresolved, and the word count lands close to the target. The opening is excellent — the gravity hiccup signaled through the drinks is a clever, show-don't-tell worldbuilding detail, and the Brin/Lio bickering establishes the cozy register immediately. The banter is sharp and economical ("An excellent dry cupboard"). The pacing is disciplined: cozy scene-setting, stranger arrives, stakes escalate in controlled increments. The plot mechanics are genuinely well-constructed. The falsified anchor assessment, the hollow seam, the drilling deadline, and especially the reveal that Nets's old Transit authorization was used — this ties the stranger's arrival directly to the protagonist's past, which is exactly what the premise demanded ("escaping from her past life"). The final beat, where the tug docks using Nets's own access code, is a strong cliffhanger that deepens rather than resolves the conflict. Character work is solid. Nets's voice is dry, deflecting, observant — consistent throughout. Her small evasions (claiming she "found the fault" rather than fixed it, refusing to explain her departure in public) give her texture. Jo, Brin, Lio, and Tam are sketched efficiently with distinct functions. Ivo Sen is a bit thin as a character — mostly a plot delivery device — but serviceable. Weaknesses: The exposition dump about the survey and seam, while handled through dialogue, is still fairly direct information transfer. Ivo's motivations remain opaque beyond "frightened messenger." The emotional complexity is present but modest — this is cozy fiction, so that's partly genre-appropriate, but Nets's internal life could be richer; her reaction to seeing her old name is mostly physical (fingers tightening). A few of the quips land slightly too neatly, edging toward sitcom rhythm. The "I can manage one of those" line is a nice touch, though. The prose is clean, controlled, and unpretentious. No purple passages, no overwrought moments. Sentences flow naturally with good variation. The ending is appropriately ominous without being melodramatic. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 56.3
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Gone South The man in the pickup lets me out beside a hotel with gold letters on the doors. He says, “This is as far as I’m going,” like I’ve been begging to ride along forever instead of the last six hours. It’s six-thirteen in the morning. My phone is at twelve percent. New Orleans smells like wet pavement, coffee, and something sweet rotting in a trash can. I thought getting out of Tennessee would feel like winning. Right now I mostly feel hungry. A streetcar rattles past, all lit up and full of people who apparently know where they’re going. I sit on a bench and check my messages, even though I know what’s there. Mom: *Please tell me where you are.* Mom: *We need to talk.* Dad: *You cannot just disappear because we had a disagreement.* A disagreement. Like we’d argued about who left dishes in the sink, and not whether they were ever going to call me their kid again. I type, *I’m alive.* Then I delete it. Mom would ask where. Dad would tell me to come home. Neither of them would ask what I needed. I put my phone away. Eleven percent. The girl on the other end of the bench says, “You look like you slept in a truck.” “That obvious?” “The seat belt mark, mostly.” I touch my neck. She’s wearing a green raincoat with one sleeve patched in yellow thread. Her hair is shaved on one side, grown out on the other. Maybe seventeen. Maybe older. I’m bad at guessing when people look like they’ve had to be older for a while. “You from here?” I ask. “Nope.” She stands. “You hungry?” Every warning I’ve ever been given wakes up at once. She sees it on my face. “Fair. There’s a breakfast place around the corner. You can watch me order and leave if I start acting weird.” “You’re already acting weird.” “Then I’m consistent.” She holds out a hand, not close enough that I have to take it. “I’m Kit.” “Taylor.” I follow her from half a block back. The place is busy enough to have a line. Kit buys two biscuits with crumpled bills from her pocket, then lets me choose which one I want. I don’t thank her until I’ve eaten half of mine, which is rude, but I’ve been saving my politeness for an emergency. “I got here yesterday,” she says. “Thought I knew somebody. Didn’t.” “That sucks.” “Yeah.” She asks where I’m from. I say Tennessee. She doesn’t ask why I left, and I like her for that more than I want to. Outside, a man playing trumpet under an awning makes the tune bend into something sad. My eyes sting. I tell myself it’s the hot sauce. By ten, the city has turned up the heat. Kit and I sit on the steps outside a public library, waiting for it to open. I’ve decided a library is a place where I can ask questions without buying anything. Kit said she was going there anyway, which might be true. “You got somebody you can call?” she asks. “Do you?” Her mouth shuts. Point taken, apparently. Inside, the air-conditioning makes my skin prickle. A librarian with silver glasses listens while I explain that I’m sixteen, I need somewhere safe to be tonight, and I’m not sure who to call. I leave out the pickup truck. I don’t know why. Maybe because saying it aloud will make me hear how lucky I was. The librarian doesn’t lecture me. She takes us to a desk away from the computers and calls a local youth-support service. While she waits on hold, she writes down their number and the library’s address. “Here,” she says, sliding the paper toward me. “Keep this in case your phone dies.” My throat tightens over a scrap of paper. Stupid throat. Kit takes the chair beside mine but doesn’t sit all the way back. She watches the doors. When the librarian asks whether both of us need help, Kit says, “Just Taylor.” The librarian nods, but I catch her looking at Kit’s raincoat, at the bag looped twice around Kit’s wrist. At noon, an outreach worker named Ms. Alvarez comes to meet us. She wears a lanyard and speaks to me like I’m capable of understanding full sentences. There may be a place for me tonight; she needs to make some calls. She explains what she can keep private and what she can’t, then asks if I want to tell her anything about home. I stare at a poster about library cards. “I’m trans,” I say. “I told my parents. It went bad.” She says, “I’m sorry. What name and pronouns should I use?” I wasn’t ready for the question. “Taylor. They and them.” “Okay, Taylor.” That’s it. Two words, no wince, no speech. I want to cry so badly I get mad instead. Kit has gone quiet. After Ms. Alvarez steps away to make a call, I ask, “What?” “Nothing.” “You’ve been looking at me funny.” “I haven’t.” “You’re doing it now.” She pulls her bag tighter. “My little brother’s trans. He told our dad last year.” “Oh.” I have a whole pile of things I could say and no idea which one won’t hurt. “He’s at my aunt’s,” she adds. “He’s okay.” She looks down. “I said I didn’t have anyone to call. I do. I just don’t want her telling my dad where I am.” It’s the first thing she’s told me that sounds completely true. “Why’d you leave?” Kit rubs at the yellow stitching on her sleeve. “I took money from his drawer. I was going to send it to my aunt. I didn’t get that far.” I think about the biscuit she bought me. “Was that his money?” “No.” She almost smiles. “That was mine.” I don’t know if I believe her. I also don’t know what I would have done this morning without her. By evening, Ms. Alvarez has arranged a safe place for me to stay while we figure out tomorrow. She asks Kit if she wants to talk too. Kit says no, then follows her into the hallway anyway. I turn my phone on for the first time in hours. Three percent. I send Mom a message: *I’m safe with someone helping me. I’m not coming home tonight. I need you to call me Taylor and listen when I’m ready.* The typing dots appear. Vanish. Appear again. My battery dies before her answer arrives. I sit with that for a minute. I want to know what she said. I’m afraid to know. Both feelings can stay, I guess; there’s room on the chair. Through the window, the evening streetcar sparks along its wire. Kit comes back and sits beside me, leaving a careful inch between us. I’m still two states from home, and I still don’t know what tomorrow is going to be like. “Did you talk to your aunt?” I ask. “Not yet.” She turns the scrap of paper Ms. Alvarez gave her over in her hands. “I got her number down, though.” I show her the folded paper in my pocket. “Me too.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a competent, controlled YA chapter with a strong, restrained first-person voice. Taylor's internal monologue is dry, defensive, and emotionally credible ("I've been saving my politeness for an emergency"). The mixed tense instruction is loosely honored—mostly present tense with occasional past-tense reflection. Kit is a well-drawn secondary character with plausible secrets and guarded disclosure; her brother reveal lands naturally. The librarian and Ms. Alvarez are refreshingly competent adults, avoiding the cliché of every adult failing the runaway. Strengths: economical prose, good subtext in dialogue, believable wariness and trust-building, the phone/battery motif used effectively, and the ending's ambiguity (typing dots, dead battery) is earned rather than saccharine. Weaknesses: the plot is low-stakes and frictionless—Taylor encounters only kindness all day; the "dangers" the prompt asks about never materialize, deflating tension. The chapter resolves toward safety and support a bit too smoothly, edging toward incongruent positivity given the setup's desperation. Some beats are predictable (kind stranger, wise librarian, outreach worker who asks pronouns perfectly). The emotional beats are handled with restraint but occasionally telegraphed ("I want to cry so badly I get mad instead" is telling). Dialogue is functional and natural but rarely surprising. Descriptive imagery is sparse and serviceable rather than vivid. The word count falls short of the 1000-word seed, though not drastically. Overall: a solid, professional piece that satisfies most instructions but plays it safe, lacking the danger, surprise, and sensory richness that would elevate it. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 80.2
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
By breakfast, the library had acquired a lake in its basement. It was a modest lake, as lakes went. The deepest part came to Midas’s knees, and nothing lived in it yet. Nevertheless, the people of the library had put their food on the upper shelves and were referring to the situation as “the flood,” which made it sound less like a maintenance problem and more like an event with a commemorative plaque. “The pump needs a battery,” Midas said. Chewy sat opposite him on the circulation desk. He was an animo-tronic stuffed koala from before the collapse, when people had apparently possessed enough electricity to teach toys to sigh. His left ear had been sewn on with fishing line. “The weather station has one,” Chewy said. “Or it had one eleven years ago, when I last saw it.” Midas spread a damp map between them. “We go through the service tunnel, take the battery, and come home.” Chewy’s eyes flickered yellow. “That means you’re worried.” “It means my eye contacts are corroded.” “They only do it when you’re worried.” “I worry about corrosion.” They left before the library residents could form a committee to discuss their departure. Midas took a sack, a crowbar, and a length of rope. Chewy took the map, on the grounds that he could read it and Midas tended to treat arrows as suggestions. The service tunnel was dry, dark, and full of signs directing authorised personnel to places that no longer existed. At the first junction, they followed a painted arrow marked **STATION ACCESS**. At the second, they followed Chewy’s map. At the third, they followed a fresh breeze. Twenty minutes later they climbed a ladder and emerged behind the library’s lending desk. Nell, who was carrying a stack of books upstairs, stopped to look at them. “Battery?” she asked. “Not yet,” said Midas. “Did you remember to bring the ladder back?” Midas looked down at the ladder. Chewy’s eyes flashed orange. They left again by the front door. The weather station stood on a hill beyond the canal, its wind rotor turning slowly above a city of low roofs and tree-filled streets. Reaching it required crossing the toll bridge. The bridge had been built for cars, but these days its chief business was sustaining three brothers who sat beneath an awning and charged travellers for using it. “What have you got?” asked the eldest. Midas showed him the crowbar. “That’ll cover you,” the brother said, reaching for it. Midas pulled it back. “I meant I’ve got a crowbar.” “And I meant I’d like one.” While they discussed the distinction, Chewy climbed onto the parapet. “Is there a charge for jumping?” The brothers looked over the side. The canal was wide and brown, with enough current to make the question interesting. “No,” said the eldest. “Good.” Chewy pointed downstream. “There’s a barge coming. We could ask for a lift.” There was indeed a barge. Midas called to it, and its owner, who knew Nell, brought it alongside. The brothers watched them board without paying. This appeared to trouble them less than the possibility that Chewy might actually have jumped. The barge took them as far as the hill. At the weather station they found the outer gate hanging open and the equipment shed locked from within. Midas rattled the door. Something rattled back. “Someone’s here,” he whispered. “Perhaps they know where the battery is.” A voice from the shed said, “Visitor acknowledged. Please wait for assistance.” They waited. No assistance came. Midas worked the crowbar into the doorframe. Before he could lean on it, the lock clicked and the door swung outward. Inside stood a waist-high maintenance machine with six wheels and one metal arm. Behind it, the battery sat beneath a bench, cables running up to the rotor. “Hello,” said Chewy. “Visitor acknowledged,” said the machine. “Please wait for assistance.” “What sort of assistance?” Midas asked. The machine raised its arm. A brush at the end swept dust from his boot. They let it finish. It was the first cleaning either of them had received that month. Then Midas disconnected the battery. The rotor slowed and stopped. So did the machine, halfway through polishing his other boot. Chewy looked at the battery. “That was easier than I expected.” Midas lifted it. “Don’t say that.” On the way out, the gate slammed shut. The sign beside it, which they had passed without reading, said **ELECTRIC RELEASE—PUSH TO OPEN**. They climbed the fence. Midas landed badly and tore his coat; Chewy caught his repaired ear on the wire and lost it altogether. They went back for it. By then the barge was gone. Rain began as they reached the canal. The battery was too heavy to carry the long way round to the bridge, so they found a maintenance skiff tied among the reeds. It leaked, but slowly. Midas rowed with a plank while Chewy bailed with his own head, which had a useful hollow beneath the ear. Halfway across, the plank broke. The current took them downstream, past the toll bridge. The three brothers waved. Midas waved back with the shorter half of the plank. They came ashore at the library’s rear loading dock, wet and an hour late. Nell met them with towels. “Battery?” she asked. Midas set it down. “Battery.” “Where’s Chewy’s ear?” Chewy held it up. “Good,” she said. “We thought you’d lost something important.” They installed the battery before supper. The pump coughed, ran for six minutes, and stopped. The basement lake had dropped by the width of a book cover. Midas went up to the roof to check the rain gutter, which had been sending fresh water straight into the foundation. Chewy followed to hold the ladder. Midas cleared a nest of leaves from the outlet; Chewy’s eyes flashed red as the gutter emptied over both of them. Midas stepped back, missed his footing, and slid down the shallow roof into a heap of wet canvas beside the front door. For the third time that day, he entered the library. Nell looked up from her books. “Finished?” “The gutter is,” Midas said. In the basement, the pump started again. Chewy came in dripping, with his ear pinned crookedly in place, and listened to it work. His eyes glowed a steady green.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of comic post-apocalyptic fiction that captures Pratchett's dry wit effectively. The story follows the requested structure precisely: deliberation over the flooded library basement, a battery-retrieval mission that goes sideways in escalating ways (emerging behind the lending desk, the toll bridge, the maintenance machine, the slammed gate, the sinking skiff), and a return home "worse for wear" — torn coat, lost ear, wet, late, and a pump that barely works. The prose is economical and wry, with excellent deadpan lines: "which made it sound less like a maintenance problem and more like an event with a commemorative plaque," and "Midas tended to treat arrows as suggestions." The dialogue between Midas and Chewy is crisp and characterful — the exchange about the flickering eyes ("It means my eye contacts are corroded") is a highlight. The maintenance machine's polite futility is a nice comic set piece, and the three toll brothers are a good recurring gag. Weaknesses: the word count is somewhat under 1000 (roughly 850), a minor adherence issue. The plot beats, while charming, are fairly conventional for this genre of comic quest — fetch item, complications, return. The ending's pump-success and green-eyed contentment is mildly tidy, though earned by the gutter fix, so it doesn't feel unearned. Nell is functional rather than nuanced. Some jokes (the ladder return) are excellent; others (the bailing with the hollow head) are slightly strained. The emotional register is consistently light — appropriate for the brief, but limits emotional complexity and depth. The world-building is implied rather than explored, which suits the length. Overall, this is confident, polished, funny writing with a consistent voice and good structural discipline. It doesn't reach the satirical density of actual Pratchett, but it's a very credible pastiche. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 56.8
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The bell over the bookshop door rang hard enough to make Nia look up from her accounts. A man in a dark coat came in sideways, shut the door behind him and crouched beneath the front window. “Please tell me there’s another way out.” “There’s the door you came in through.” “A different one.” Nia followed his gaze to the two photographers hurrying along Morgan Arcade. Beyond the glass roof, rain blurred the afternoon light. One photographer stopped to peer into the window. “There’s a staff door,” she said. The man’s face brightened. “You’re wonderful.” “It leads to a cupboard.” “Less wonderful.” “I haven’t decided what you’re running from.” “People with cameras. They’re taking my picture without asking.” “They’re taking everyone’s picture without asking. You’re the only one crawling about my carpet.” He stood, brushed a hand over his coat and offered her a smile polished to a shine. Nia knew the face now. Kit Vale, star of *The Last Kingdom of Summer*, which had filled the bus shelters from here to Cardiff Bay. “Kit Vale,” he said, as though she might have been waiting for an introduction. “Nia Morgan.” She turned a page in her ledger. “Mind the poetry display.” “Nice to meet you too, Nia.” She had meant to sound cool. Unfortunately, up close he was even better-looking than the bus shelter suggested. His hair was damp, his eyes were very blue, and his smile had slipped a little when she’d gone back to her accounts. Nia read the same column of figures for the third time. A camera flashed through the window. “Could I stay a minute?” he asked. “You can stay until they leave. Don’t stand in front of the window.” He moved obediently behind a shelf of Welsh histories. “Thank you. I can buy something.” “You don’t have to pay for shelter.” “I’d like to. What do you recommend?” “That depends. What do you read?” “Scripts, mostly.” “Then you’re due a book.” His laugh came quickly. “You’re enjoying this.” “A bit.” “I knew it. You do like me.” “I said I was enjoying this.” For the first time, he seemed unsure what to do with his hands. He pulled a paperback from the shelf. “*A Short History of Cardiff*. Good?” “Very. You’re holding it upside down.” He turned it over. “I was testing you.” “Of course.” Outside, the photographers moved toward the far end of the arcade. Kit watched them through a gap in the books. “Did you have an event nearby?” Nia asked. “A press thing at a hotel by the castle. I left through the kitchen, which usually works, but someone had the bright idea of posting pictures while I was still inside.” He looked back at her. “You knew who I was.” “I worked it out.” “And yet you let me suffer.” “You’ve been here two minutes.” “Long minutes.” She reached beneath the counter for a cloth and wiped rainwater from a stack of returned books. Anything to keep her hands occupied. “You could have stayed at the hotel.” “I wanted to see Cardiff without being escorted through it.” “Crouching behind local history isn’t seeing much of it.” “I’ve seen a bookshop. It’s a start.” He came closer, holding the history book against his chest. There was a small nick beside his jaw, missed by whoever had shaved him for the cameras. Nia looked down at the stack. “Is this your place?” he asked. “Mine and the bank’s.” “How long?” “Six years.” “I bet everyone who comes in tells you what a lovely shop it is.” “They do.” “It is a lovely shop.” “I know.” He grinned, but she caught the glance he gave her afterward, searching her face for some reward. Nia felt a ridiculous urge to give him one. “Do people usually laugh sooner?” she asked. “They usually laugh at the first thing I say.” “Is that why you keep trying?” His thumb worried the corner of the paperback. “That obvious?” “To someone standing behind a counter, yes. I see a lot of people trying to be liked.” “And you?” “I’m generally trying to sell them a book.” “Cruel woman.” “It’s a business.” The bell rang. Kit ducked so fast he nearly took the histories with him. An elderly customer stepped in, shook out her umbrella and headed straight for the gardening section. “Afternoon, Nia,” she called. “Afternoon, Mrs Price. New roses book’s on the bottom shelf.” Mrs Price waved and disappeared around the corner. Kit slowly stood. “She didn’t notice me,” he whispered. “She came for roses.” “Now I’m offended.” Nia covered her mouth with the cloth. He saw it. “There,” he said softly. “A laugh.” “You nearly demolished a shelf.” “I’ll take it.” A flush climbed her neck. She busied herself folding the cloth into quarters. “If you want a recommendation, put that history down.” “I thought you said it was very good.” “It is. I think you’ll read two pages and spend the rest of the journey wondering whether I liked you.” He opened his mouth, then closed it. His smile, when it returned, was smaller. “That’s embarrassingly fair.” Nia went to a shelf near the back and brought him a slim novel. “Try this. A man inherits a house he doesn’t want. He comes to Wales to sell it.” “And?” “He stays longer than planned.” “Do you approve of him?” “Not at first.” Kit took the book from her. Their fingers touched at the spine. It was nothing—less than a second—but Nia felt it all the way to her elbow. “What changes your mind?” he asked. “He stops performing for the neighbours. Starts listening to them.” Kit looked at the cover, then at her. “Sounds difficult.” “It takes him most of the book.” From the gardening section, Mrs Price called, “Nia, have you got change for a twenty?” “In a moment.” Nia stepped behind the counter. “Are you buying that?” “Yes. Though you’ve made it sound suspiciously like homework.” “You asked.” “I did.” He brought it over and watched her ring it up. “If I come back and tell you what I thought, will you believe I read it?” “I’ll ask you about the ending.” “And if I get it wrong?” “I’ll sell you another.” He paid. Outside, the photographers were gone, and the arcade’s glass roof showed a narrow strip of clearing sky. Kit tucked the book inside his coat. “You know, I came in here looking for a way out.” “You’ve found one.” Nia nodded toward the door. “I can see that.” He stayed where he was a moment longer. “Thank you for letting me hide.” “You’re welcome, Kit.” Her use of his name caught him off guard. Nia enjoyed that, too. At the door, he glanced back. “I’ll come by when I’ve finished it.” “Take your time.” He smiled. “I don’t think I will.” The bell gave a gentler ring as he left. Nia watched him walk down the arcade with his collar up and her book held safely under his coat. “Nia,” Mrs Price called again, “my change?” “Yes. Sorry.” Nia opened the till, still looking toward the door. “I’ve got it.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong scene that fulfills the brief with impressive economy. The dialogue is the engine, as requested, and both voices are distinct: Kit's quick, needy charm and Nia's dry deflections. The characterizations match the specification precisely — Kit's fragile ego shows in his searching for approval after jokes ("he grinned, but she caught the glance he gave her afterward, searching her face for some reward"), and Nia's inner fluster is shown through small physical beats (rereading figures, folding the cloth, the flush at her neck) rather than told. The Mrs Price interruption is an excellent comedic device that punctures Kit's ego ("She didn't notice me") while giving Nia a genuine laugh. The chemistry builds credibly: the recommended novel functions as a subtle mirror of Kit's situation, giving the attraction thematic grounding and an organic reason for a return visit. The ending's lightness feels earned because the emotional shift is incremental — no sudden confessions, just a book, a touched hand, a first name. Weaknesses are minor. The premise (celebrity hiding from paparazzi in a quirky shop) is well-trodden territory, and some beats (holding the book upside down, fingers touching on the spine) are genre clichés. The prose is clean but rarely rises above functional; imagery is sparse — Morgan Arcade's glass roof is the main sensory anchor, and even that is lightly done. Kit's "I don't think I will" is a touch pat. A few exchanges could be trimmed. None of these flaws significantly undermine the piece's wit, pacing, or emotional credibility, but they keep it from masterpiece level. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 73.4
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
Aya put her palm against the underhold door. Its iron was cold enough to ache through her glove. “No voices,” Katra whispered. “No boots,” said Simeon. He held up the key they had taken from the quartermaster. “That’s what troubles me.” Beyond them, the guild house groaned with the disorder of an arrest: men shouting over ledgers, drawers being forced, somebody demanding to know who had taken the cashbox. Here, below the wharf, there was only the slow knock of water against the foundations. Aya turned the key. The lock yielded so readily that Simeon shut his eyes. The underhold opened onto a chamber of dressed black stone. Gas lamps burned in wall cages, their flames flickering in a draught Aya could not feel. They cast long, unsettling shadows across the stone floor. At the far end, beneath the vaulted ribs of an old dry dock, stood the Scythan artifact: a dark sphere suspended within three brass rings. Its surface seemed wet, though nothing dripped from it. Between Aya and the sphere sat Mrs. Voss. The leader of the Morska guild wore her grey morning coat and the narrow-brimmed hat she had worn at yesterday’s accounts. A pistol lay across her knees. Another rested on the table at her elbow beside a pot of tea. Four bodyguards stood along the walls, shotguns lowered but ready; a fifth waited by the door with a length of chain. Mrs. Voss looked up from her cup. “I thought it might be you.” Katra stopped short. Simeon’s key fell from his hand and rang against the stones. “They took you,” Katra said. “They took my hat and a woman who looked poorly in it.” Mrs. Voss set down her cup. “The constables will discover the error once her face is washed. By then I hope to have settled my affairs.” The guard beside the door drew it shut. Iron struck iron. Aya heard the bolt slide home. She could have reached for the immateria. She felt it already, a pressure beyond the chamber, eager to pour through whatever crack she gave it. But the guards had room to fire, and Katra stood directly in front of one barrel. Aya kept her hands where they could be seen. “You arranged the raid,” she said. “I arranged a raid. Constables prefer to believe the particulars are their own.” Mrs. Voss rose. “It loosened a great many tongues upstairs. And sent three enterprising souls straight to my cellar.” Katra glanced at the sphere. “If you wanted us, you could’ve asked.” “Would you have come?” “No.” “Then I have spared us all some bother.” Mrs. Voss nodded to the guards. “Hands.” A shotgun lifted. Katra raised hers first, her face hard with the effort of it. Simeon followed. Aya waited one breath too long; the guard behind her caught her wrists and bound them with a thin steel cuff. He tightened it until her fingers tingled. No one struck her. The restraint felt deliberate, and worse for that. Mrs. Voss approached. “The mask, please.” Aya held still as the woman unhooked the black velvet and drew it away. Recognition came slowly. Mrs. Voss’s eyes passed over Aya’s face once, then returned to it. Across the room, Simeon made a small, wretched sound. “Oh,” said Mrs. Voss. “That is worth considerably more than the sphere.” Aya had spent months taking carriages home before dawn, changing in a locked room while her maid slept, sitting at breakfast with dock soot still lodged beneath her nails. She had imagined discovery often enough. In none of those imaginings had she felt so absurdly exposed by the bare skin around her mouth. Katra leaned forward. “Leave her name out of this.” “I haven’t said it.” “You’re about to.” Mrs. Voss studied Aya. “Lady Aya Vale.” The gas lamps hissed. Aya thought of her father reading that name in a constable’s report. She thought of the portrait of her mother in the upstairs hall, taken down after the hanging, its pale rectangle still visible on the wallpaper. There would be no taking down a story once Morska learned it. “Your Grace,” Simeon murmured, forgetting, in his fright, that the title was wrong. Mrs. Voss heard him. “And she kept you ignorant, did she?” “Not entirely,” Aya said. “Simeon knew enough to help me get through the first ward.” Simeon stared at her. She had just confessed to reaching the underhold, to him assisting her. But the guards had found the key. Lying about that would buy no one anything. Mrs. Voss glanced towards the sphere. “The wards I know how to mend. It’s the other thing you do that concerns me.” Aya felt Katra turn towards her. They all knew what the other thing was. They had seen her call shapes out of empty air when escape seemed impossible. None of them knew whether she could dismiss one if it chose to stay. “It concerns me as well,” Aya said. “Your mother ought to have considered it.” The words landed with such familiar cruelty that Aya nearly answered them on instinct. Instead she looked at the pistol on the table. Mrs. Voss had kept it within reach while approaching her. For all her composure, she was afraid. “You cannot afford to kill me,” Aya said. Mrs. Voss’s mouth tightened. “I can afford it rather easily.” “Not quietly. My father knows I was out last night. He will send people looking. If I vanish on the morning of a raid, they’ll turn this district over.” “Your father would sooner bury the question.” “He might. But first he would need to know whether I could speak.” Aya swallowed. “Keep me alive, and you have a hostage who can persuade him to leave Morska alone. Send him proof I’m here. Ask for passage, coin, whatever this morning’s raid has cost you.” Katra gave a faint shake of her head. Aya understood: don’t give her a price to put on you. Yet Mrs. Voss was listening. “And your friends?” Mrs. Voss asked. “They come with me. They’ve seen your cellar and your little deception. Alive, under guard, they’re useful. Dead, they’re evidence somebody may find.” “How nobly you bargain.” “I’m frightened,” Aya said. “I’ve had to think quickly.” For a moment Mrs. Voss said nothing. Then the sphere behind her made a sound like a nail drawn across a tooth. Simeon flinched. One of the brass rings had begun to turn. Mrs. Voss looked back at it. “It started doing that when you came in.” Aya watched the dark surface. She could feel something within it attending to her, as distinctly as she felt the cuff bite her wrists. Her mother had known what lived beyond the sensible world and had died with people calling that knowledge a crime. Now Mrs. Voss knew her daughter had inherited it. “Then,” Aya said, keeping her voice level, “you may have another reason to keep me.” Mrs. Voss considered the turning ring. At last she motioned the guards away from the door. “Cells for all three,” she said. “Separate ones. Lady Vale gets paper and ink.” Katra met Aya’s eyes as they were led out. There was anger there, and fear, but she was still walking. Aya held on to that as the underhold door opened and the noisy guild house swallowed them again.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece executes the prompt's beats competently: the trio enters the underhold, finds Mrs. Voss un-incarcerated with bodyguards, Aya is captured and unmasked, and she negotiates her value as a hostage while grappling with exposure. No fight scene occurs, third person past tense is maintained, internal monologue is present (the pale rectangle on the wallpaper, the imagined discoveries), and dialogue carries much of the scene. Strengths: The prose is controlled and economical, with a dry, period-appropriate register ("They took my hat and a woman who looked poorly in it"). Mrs. Voss is a genuinely good creation — her composure, the tea, the small tell of keeping the pistol within reach. The double-deception of the arrest (a body double) is a clever, believable twist that explains her freedom without contrivance. The artifact reacting to Aya's presence adds gothic dread efficiently. The negotiation is tense and the hostage logic is coherent. Weaknesses: The dialogue, while serviceable, occasionally flattens into functional exchanges ("Hands." / "Would you have come?" / "No.") that read more like blocking than character. Katra and Simeon are thinly differentiated; Simeon's "Your Grace" error is a nice touch but he remains mostly a flinching prop. The gothic horror elements are gestured at rather than fully inhabited — the sphere's "nail drawn across a tooth" is the strongest moment, but the immateria's menace stays abstract. The ending resolves a shade too neatly: Mrs. Voss capitulates to the hostage argument rather quickly, and "Lady Vale gets paper and ink" wraps the standoff with less cost than the scene's stakes seemed to demand. The emotional complexity of Aya's unmasking is told more than felt in places ("so absurdly exposed"). The Victorian texture is present but not especially vivid — brass, gas lamps, wharf — hitting expected notes without surprise. Overall this is a solid, professional genre scene with a strong antagonist and clean structure, held back by thin secondary characters, dialogue that is competent rather than distinctive, and a resolution that arrives slightly too easily.
