Prompt:
**"Breaking Formation"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a street dancer from a rough neighborhood who's won a scholarship to an elite K-pop training academy in Seoul. Desperately out of place culturally and technically, they struggle with a militaristically precise choreography that contradicts everything about their improvisational background. The punishing rehearsal takes place under a famous instructor known for breaking students to remake them, who sees potential in the narrator's raw talent but not their attitude. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—each dance move, position shift, and spatial relationship must be tracked with precision throughout the studio. Paint an exceptionally vivid kinetic picture through descriptions that capture not just movement but the contrast between the narrator's fluid, expressive style and the mechanical precision demanded. Their internal monologue should reveal culture shock, class anxiety, and the threatening realization that success here might mean losing their authentic movement voice. Include technical terminology that highlights the collision of street and commercial styles, moments when muscle memory betrays them, and a crucial decision point about whether to conform or rebel. Physical clarity is essential—readers must be able to visualize exactly how bodies move through space, how rhythms align or clash, and how the protagonist's body struggles against unfamiliar discipline. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The studio had a speaker in each corner, all four blasting the same beat just a hair too loud. The bass hit my ribs before it reached my ears. I stood on a blue tape cross in the front row, left of center, facing the north wall of mirrors. Jiwoo stood a meter and a half to my right; Min stood the same distance beyond her. Three more trainees filled the row behind us. The mirrors made six dancers into twelve, but the tape told the truth about where everyone belonged. My sneakers had a split in the sole. Jiwoo’s looked as if they had come out of the box that morning. I kept mine planted over the cross so nobody would see. “From one,” said Madam Kang. Even back home in Chicago, I knew her name. People posted clips of her rehearsals with captions about how she broke trainees down and built idols out of the pieces. Up close, she was smaller than I expected. She stood by the mirror, north and a little left of my mark, with her arms folded. The count began in Korean. I knew the numbers now. My body still waited for English. On one, my right foot had to step thirty centimeters right, toward Jiwoo. On two, my left foot closed beside it. On three, right foot forward toward the mirror; four, left foot closed. Five sent the right foot back to the row line, six brought the left after it. Seven sent the left foot back to my original cross; eight brought the right beside it. A square with one side missing. Simple, if you thought feet were all a dancer had. Every landing had an arm position. Right elbow level with shoulder on one. Both forearms flat across the chest on two. Hands punched overhead on three, then snapped to the hips on four. Kang wanted our shoulders still and our weight centered, so that all six bodies struck the same shapes at the same instant. “Again.” The track started. My right foot landed on one. Jiwoo’s landed beside it, exactly level with mine. By two, my left foot had closed, but my chest was already rolling through the bass. It was a small thing, a wave under my sweatshirt. In the park by the train tracks, I would have let it run down through my knees, caught the next snare in my heel, maybe dropped low enough for somebody to shout. Here, the roll made my elbows arrive late. Kang cut the music before three. My face heated. The trainee behind me lowered his eyes to my shoes, then raised them to the mirror. He was being polite. Somehow that was worse. “Your feet,” Kang said, “are almost correct.” Almost. The scholarship letter on my mother’s fridge had sounded so absolute. *Full tuition.* It had not mentioned the meals I ate alone because conversation moved too fast, or the other trainees’ effortless changes between Korean and English, or the price of one pair of their practice shoes. Kang stepped away from the mirror and stopped about a meter in front of me, still between me and my reflection. “Where did this come from?” She traced the path of my chest roll with two fingers in the air. “The beat.” “The beat is not asking you.” Nobody laughed. That made it worse, too. She returned to her place by the mirror. “From one.” This time I locked my sternum down. Right, close, forward, close. My arms hit their positions. Five, back. Six, close. On seven, as my left foot moved left toward the cross, the snare opened a little space. My left shoulder followed it. I could feel a glide waiting there, the sort that made my feet seem to stick while my body traveled. Muscle memory took the invitation. My shoulder slid left; my head stayed behind; my right foot arrived on eight a fraction late. The music stopped. Jiwoo, still on her own tape, looked at me in the mirror. She didn’t look angry. She looked tired. “You hear things the others don’t,” Kang said. “I can see that.” Hope rose so fast it hurt. “But you keep answering them when no one has called on you.” She came forward again. This time she stood just to my left, leaving the mirror clear, and tapped the floor at the edge of my cross. “Seven ends here. Eight ends here. If you take Jiwoo’s space, she has to adjust. Then Min adjusts. You think you are dancing alone because that is how you learned.” I looked right. The empty floor between Jiwoo and me suddenly seemed narrow. At home, a circle opened to give you room. Here, room was something other people had measured and trusted you not to steal. Kang walked back north. “One last time.” The speakers cracked with the opening bass. My knees wanted to loosen. I held them ready instead. One: right foot right, elbow up. Two: left beside it, forearms flat. Three: right foot toward the mirror, fists high. Four: left foot in, hands at hips. In the glass, six pairs of hands arrived together. Five: right foot back. Six: left beside it. The snare was coming. On seven I sent my left foot left, exactly onto the cross. My shoulder wanted to follow. I could clamp it still. I could become the clean outline Kang wanted and let the rest of me disappear inside it. Or I could make Jiwoo move again. I kept my shoulder square. On eight my right foot closed on time. At the instant both soles met, I let my fingers open at my sides—no arm swing, no step off the mark. Just a quick release through my hands, like letting go of a breath. By the next one, they were fists again. Kang heard it, somehow. Her gaze found mine in the mirror. “Again,” she said. This time, she didn’t stop the music.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a disciplined, tightly controlled piece that fulfills the prompt's central demands with unusual precision. The spatial tracking is exemplary: the blue tape cross, the meter-and-a-half spacing between dancers, the square footwork pattern broken down count-by-count, and Kang's repositioning around the narrator are all legible and consistent. The choreography is described in genuinely countable terms (right foot thirty centimeters right on one, close on two, etc.), which delivers the "physical coherence" requirement better than most attempts at this kind of scene. The central conflict—improvisational street instinct versus militaristic precision—is dramatized through concrete kinetic detail rather than abstract statement. The chest roll that makes elbows arrive late, the shoulder glide on seven that delays the right foot on eight, and the final compromise (fingers opening at the sides while feet stay on the mark) are all excellent "muscle memory betrays them" moments. The ending's small rebellion—releasing through the hands without breaking formation—is a genuinely earned decision point, neither full capitulation nor full rebellion, and Kang's response ("This time, she didn't stop the music") is a subtle, satisfying beat of acknowledgment. Class anxiety and culture shock are handled with restraint: the split sole versus box-fresh sneakers, the scholarship letter on the fridge, eating alone, the code-switching trainees. The line "The beat is not asking you" is a strong, characterful piece of dialogue for Kang. The narrator's internal monologue about circles opening at home versus measured, trusted floor space here is one of the piece's best observations—spatial thinking used to carry cultural meaning. Weaknesses: the piece is somewhat short of the 1000-word seed (roughly 850), and its compression occasionally works against it. The supporting trainees (Jiwoo, Min) are barely individuated—Jiwoo gets a tired look and new shoes, nothing more. Kang, while effectively drawn, stays within the familiar archetype of the severe instructor who sees potential; there's little that surprises about her. The prose is clean but deliberately flat in places; some sentences ("Hope rose so fast it hurt") edge toward stock phrasing. The technical terminology is lighter than requested—there's little street-style vocabulary (no popping, locking, freestyle terminology) to collide with the K-pop counting language, which the prompt explicitly asked for. The emotional register is controlled to the point of slight monotony; the piece never quite erupts, and while that restraint is thematically apt, it limits the emotional range. The ending is quietly hopeful but appropriately so—not incongruent. Overall, this is a skilled, coherent, well-structured piece that hits most of its marks with precision, held back from excellence by thin secondary characters, limited stylistic range, and a slightly underdeveloped technical vocabulary. + Gothic-fantasy-humour: Court of the Dreaming — Score: 85.9
Prompt:
Court of the Dreaming: Territorial Dream Dispute. Write a dark fantasy scene with comedic elements set in the Courts of Dream where a case is being heard to determine ownership of a contested dreamscape. Mora, the Slavic nightmare spirit who sits on sleepers' chests causing paralysis and terror, has recently invaded and subverted a carefully crafted recurring dream of a schoolboy, Max. The dream originally featured the boy lying in a field of wildflowers with his crush, always culminating in a muddled almost-kiss and a pleasant confusion of emotions. This dream was the meticulous work of "First Love" (a rosy-cheeked, slightly bashful entity who crafts formative romantic experiences). However, Mora has recently infiltrated the dreamscape, transforming the scene so that when the girl playfully mounts the boy, she morphs into a terrifying yet somehow still confusingly attractive vision who proceeds to sit on his chest and feed on his breath. Mora's defense largely consists of the practical argument that "a girl's gotta eat too, you know?" Write this scene as it unfolds in the courtroom of the Dreaming, with Dream's demeanour, typically impenetrable, betraying a sense of irritation at having to adjudicate such matters. The comedy should derive from the farcical situation, familiar elements of courtroom drama intersecting with the fantastical world of the Dreaming, and the droll portrayal of the characters and their interactions. The humor should be dark and understated throughout. Dream is tempted to some mischief in the resolution of the case. Use descriptives sparingly when setting scene. Write for readability & engagement. 1000 words.
Model Output:
A single, giant hourglass in the courtroom dripped shimmering sand. “Case four hundred and twelve,” said the clerk. “First Love versus Mora. Disputed occupation of a recurring dream.” Dream sat behind the bench with his hands folded. His face gave nothing away. Only the pen in his hand, which had stopped moving some time ago, suggested that the proceedings had tested him. First Love rose. He had rosy cheeks, ink on his cuffs, and a folder tied with pink ribbon. “I made the dream,” he said. “Every part of it.” “You may describe the property,” said Dream. “A field of wildflowers. Late afternoon. Max lies beside a girl from his school. They talk about things neither of them will remember in the morning. She leans closer. He does too. They never quite kiss.” “Why not?” asked Mora. First Love’s cheeks deepened. “Because he isn’t ready.” Mora made a soft, skeptical noise. “It’s a good dream,” First Love said. “He wakes up happy and terribly confused. I adjusted the weather for six weeks to get that right.” The clerk held up a document. “The original design has been entered as Exhibit A.” From the folder rose the smell of grass, then the distant sound of two children laughing. For a moment, even the gallery of nightmares fell quiet. “And Exhibit B?” asked Dream. The clerk hesitated. “We have a statement from the sleeper.” “Read it.” “‘I was in the flower field again. We were messing around, and she climbed onto me to stop me getting up. Then her face changed. I couldn’t move. Something sat on my chest and took my breath. When I woke up, I could still feel the weight.’” The clerk turned the page. “‘I don’t want to go back there.’” First Love looked down at his folder. Mora crossed her legs. In her chosen shape she resembled an old woman made of smoke and patience, though her shadow had a different set of teeth. “A girl’s gotta eat too, you know?” she said. Dream looked at her. “That,” he said, “is your defense?” “It’s the short version.” “I had hoped.” Mora spread her hands. “Sleepers have grown difficult. Locks on doors, lights left burning, little machines that play rain all night. This boy comes along with a door he opens willingly, three nights a week. Am I supposed to walk past it?” “Yes,” said First Love. “You would say that. You don’t have to find your own supper.” Dream turned to the clerk. “Is there a longer version?” “Seventeen pages, my lord.” “Give me the short one again.” Mora leaned forward. “I did not destroy his dream. The flowers are still there. The girl is still there, at first. I added a turn he didn’t expect.” “You used her face,” said First Love. “He trusted her.” “I used what the dream gave me.” “You used what I gave him.” Mora’s eyes narrowed. “There it is. You think because you planted the field, everything in it belongs to you.” First Love opened his mouth, then closed it. Dream set down his pen. The small sound carried through the court. “Neither of you owns Max,” he said. “Though I begin to understand why he sleeps so badly.” The clerk coughed into his sleeve. At the back, a creature with antlers hastily lowered a placard reading *PRECEDENT?* Dream noticed. The creature hid it behind its chair. “Call the next witness,” Dream said. “There is no next witness, my lord.” “Then why,” Dream asked, “have we reserved the court until dawn?” The clerk consulted the docket. “Mora requested time to demonstrate the feeding.” “No,” said Dream. “It might clarify—” “It would not.” Mora shrugged, as though this were the court’s loss. First Love untied his folder and drew out a sketch of the field. Tiny notes ran along its edges: *wind light enough to lift hair; avoid bees; allow silence after joke*. One corner had been worn thin by handling. “I know dreams change,” he said. “I know they aren’t safe just because I made them. But he liked going there. Now he’s afraid to sleep in case it comes back.” For once, Mora said nothing. Dream examined the sketch. A narrow path crossed the field, vanishing beyond the paper’s edge. Max had made that part himself. “Your claim,” Dream told Mora, “rests on access. His claim rests on prior work. Both are weaker than the sleeper’s wish not to return.” Mora straightened. “So I starve.” “No. There are other sleepers.” “Most of them wake as soon as I arrive.” “You may find,” said Dream, “that a less recognizable entrance helps.” His gaze drifted to the gallery. The antlered creature slid lower in its chair. Beside it sat Mr. Parch, advocate for the Guild of Night Terrors, who had spent the hearing passing notes to Mora and nodding whenever anyone said *jurisdiction*. Dream considered him for a moment. His expression remained solemn, but the clerk knew that look. It had preceded several rulings no one had enjoyed carrying out. “Mora is barred from Max’s flower field,” Dream said. “She will restore the dream to its condition before her entry. First Love may tend it, but he will leave room for Max to change it.” First Love nodded quickly. “Of course.” “And the girl,” Dream added, “may do as she likes.” First Love looked startled. “She always could.” Dream glanced at the sketch, at the careful note marking exactly when she should lean closer. First Love quietly folded it away. “As to Mora’s need to feed,” Dream continued, “the court will grant her access to an unoccupied territory with a reliable supply of dread.” Mr. Parch sat up. “My lord, which territory?” “The dreams of those who petition this court for damages.” The advocate went still. The clerk’s quill scratched across the order. “Beginning when, my lord?” Dream picked up his pen again. “Tonight. Mr. Parch has a hearing tomorrow, and I would prefer him alert.” A few nightmares laughed before they could stop themselves. Mora showed her teeth. She looked quite pleased with the arrangement. As the court emptied, First Love stayed by the bench. “Will Max go back?” he asked. “I don’t know,” said Dream. First Love gathered his folder. “I suppose I can wait.” “For once,” said Dream, “that would be wise.” Above them, sand fell through the hourglass. Somewhere, a boy slept undisturbed, and the field waited for him.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong execution of the prompt. The scene delivers the courtroom farce with understated dark humor: Dream's irritation is conveyed economically (the stopped pen, "I had hoped"), Mora's "a girl's gotta eat" defense is handled with dry wit, and the resolution—Dream sentencing Mora to haunt the dreams of those who petition the court, targeting Mr. Parch specifically—is a clever, mischievous twist that fulfills the "tempted to mischief" instruction. First Love's sketch with marginal notes ("wind light enough to lift hair; avoid bees") is a lovely show-don't-tell detail that characterizes him instantly. The sleeper's statement grounds the comedy in genuine harm, giving the piece emotional weight. Prose is spare and controlled, dialogue crisp. Minor weaknesses: the ending's "a boy slept undisturbed, and the field waited" is slightly more sentimental than the rest of the piece warrants, and the antlered creature with the "PRECEDENT?" placard is a touch cute. Overall, well-earned darkness and lightness, coherent, engaging. + Fanfic-crossover: Blood Moon — Score: 58.7
Prompt:
Blood Moon Alucard & Yennefer Write a story where Alucard (Hellsing) encounters Yennefer (The Witcher) in medieval Europe. Yennefer's magical abilities intrigue the vampire, while she's both repulsed and fascinated by his monstrous nature. Their power dynamic shifts constantly as they circle each other, neither willing to show weakness first. **Alucard (Hellsing)** Alucard is an ancient, immensely powerful vampire who works for the Hellsing Organization. He can regenerate from almost any wound and shape-shift at will. He's sadistic, arrogant, and takes pleasure in toying with his enemies before killing them. Despite being a monster, he despises weak vampires who can't accept their nature. He wears a distinctive red coat, wide-brimmed hat, and orange sunglasses. He uses massive handguns loaded with silver bullets. He seeks worthy opponents who can challenge him and potentially end his immortal existence. Famous quote: "The bird of Hermes is my name, eating my wings to make me tame." **Yennefer of Vengerberg (The Witcher)** Yennefer is a powerful sorceress who magically altered her appearance to hide her congenital hunchback. She's ambitious, stubborn, and manipulative when necessary. She has violet eyes and smells of lilac and gooseberries. Despite her cold exterior, she desperately wants to reverse her infertility caused by magical transformation. She's centuries old but appears young. She's politically savvy and refuses to be underestimated. She has a sarcastic sense of humor and little patience for fools. Though she rarely shows it, she's capable of deep love and loyalty. Famous quote: "I'm not sweet and I'm not a maiden in distress in need of saving." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Blood Moon A broken cart wheel lies abandoned near the village gates. Its axle has been torn clean through, and the road beyond is scored by hoofprints heading west. Whoever fled did not stop to repair it. Yennefer steps over the wheel and looks up at the moon. Red light washes the thatched roofs, the empty market stalls, the chapel bell. The village should be sleeping. Instead, every door stands open. A man in a red coat waits beside the well. “You’re late,” he says. “I wasn’t aware we had an appointment.” Behind orange lenses, his smile widens. He is absurdly dressed for a village on the edge of a Bohemian forest: broad hat, scarlet coat, polished boots. At his hips hang two handguns so large they look like an insult to the age. Yennefer smells blood beneath the cold air. A great deal of it. “Where are the villagers?” she asks. “Some fled. Some are in the chapel.” “Alive?” “That depends on how quickly you learn to ask useful questions.” She closes her fist. The stones around his boots split, and iron-hard roots burst through them, twisting around his ankles. He looks down. “Better.” The roots tighten. Bone cracks. His smile does not falter. Yennefer lets the spell hold while she studies him. No heartbeat. No breath. The shape of a man occupied by something vast and hungry. She has met vampires before, but their presence feels like a blade held close to the skin. His feels like standing at the edge of a pit and discovering the pit is looking back. “You’re the one who emptied the village,” she says. “No.” He pulls one foot free. Flesh knits around the bone before her eyes. “I’m the one who found what did.” The chapel bell rings once. Neither of them has touched it. Yennefer turns. Shadows move behind the chapel windows, too many to belong to the villagers who remain. A thin voice begins to sing inside, then breaks off. The vampire draws a gun. “Silver,” Yennefer says, catching a glimpse of the cartridges. “How observant.” “It won’t stop me.” “I know.” He fires. She throws up a shield. The shot strikes it like a hammer, driving her back a step. Before she can retaliate, something drops from the roof behind her. Alucard fires again, past her shoulder. A pale figure hits the mud, its head reduced to fragments. It keeps crawling. Yennefer burns it to ash. For a moment they stand side by side, watching the remains drift across the square. “Newly made,” Alucard says, with contempt. “They think hunger is all it takes.” “Who made them?” “Someone hiding in the chapel.” “Then why are you out here entertaining yourself?” He turns his head toward her. “I was waiting to see whether you were part of it.” “And?” “I haven’t decided.” The air folds around Yennefer. She steps through it and appears at the chapel doors, leaving his gun pointed at empty space. She hears him laugh behind her. Inside, candles burn with black flames. Villagers lie bound between the pews, conscious but drained and too weak to cry out. At the altar stands a woman wearing a priest’s stolen vestments. Fresh blood darkens her mouth. The woman lifts a knife toward a bound boy. “One more,” she whispers, “and the moon will make me—” Yennefer tears the knife from her hand without moving. “Whatever you hope it will make you,” she says, “it won’t.” The woman shrieks. Figures unfold from the rafters and fall upon Yennefer in a tangle of claws. Her shield flares violet. It holds for one breath, two. Then the chapel doors explode inward. Alucard walks through splintered oak and fires until the pews are burning and the things that fell from the rafters are no longer recognizable. He does not spare a glance for the villagers pinned beneath them. “Mind the living,” Yennefer snaps. “Then move them.” She does. With a sweep of her hand she drags the villagers, ropes and all, behind the stone font. The effort costs her a heartbeat of concentration. The woman at the altar sees it. She throws a fistful of blood into the black flames. They rise together, forming a writhing shape that fills the chapel from floor to beams. Yennefer feels the working catch at the edges of her mind. It is crude, but it has been fed by every life taken here. The candles go out. The font cracks. Alucard’s grin vanishes. At last, Yennefer thinks, something he respects. The shape strikes. He takes the blow full in the chest, and the red coat bursts apart. Darkness pours from him in answer: eyes opening in it, jaws snapping, shadows crowding every wall. The villagers whimper behind the font. Yennefer recoils despite herself. She sees no end to what he holds inside. Whatever has worn a human face to meet her at the well has done so by choice. “Repulsed?” his voice asks from everywhere. “Yes.” She plants her feet. “You’re also in my way.” She drives a spell through him and into the blood-fire beyond. It pins his shadows to the chapel stones. For an instant his monstrous form cannot move, and the thing at the altar thrashes against the force of her will. Alucard could tear free. She feels him test the binding. Instead, he holds still. Yennefer understands. She draws the stolen blood out of the flames, a dark ribbon that coils around her raised hand. The woman screams as her spell collapses. Alucard’s shadows close over what remains. When silence returns, Yennefer releases her binding. Her hand trembles once before she lowers it. He sees; she knows he does. But he is still standing where she held him, and neither mentions that. Outside, dawn has begun to pale the red moon. Alucard waits by the broken cart wheel while the villagers stumble west along the road. “You could have warned me,” Yennefer says. “You wouldn’t have come.” She cannot deny it. “You could have killed her yourself.” “I did.” “After I made it possible.” His smile returns, smaller this time. “Yes.” Yennefer walks past him. Lilac and gooseberries linger briefly in the cold air. “Are you following me?” she asks without looking back. “Would you stop me?” She considers the vast shadow at her back, and the moment in the chapel when he chose to trust her hands around it. “Try it,” she says. His laughter follows her through the gates, but his footsteps do not.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece successfully executes the prompt: third-person present tense throughout, medieval European setting, and the core dynamic of two monsters circling each other with a constantly shifting power balance. Both characters are recognizably themselves — Alucard's theatrical menace, contempt for weak vampires, and hunger for a worthy opponent come through in his sparse dialogue ("Better." / "Newly made. They think hunger is all it takes."); Yennefer's sarcasm, refusal to be underestimated, and hidden vulnerability (the trembling hand he notices but doesn't mention) are all handled with restraint. The prose is notably disciplined. Short declarative sentences create tension without becoming choppy, and imagery is concrete and earned: "his presence feels like a blade held close to the skin. His feels like standing at the edge of a pit and discovering the pit is looking back" is the standout line, showing Yennefer's expertise through comparison. The "repulsed but fascinated" dynamic is dramatized rather than stated — she recoils, admits "Yes," then refuses to move anyway. The plot structure is efficient: a mystery (empty village), a bait-and-switch (Alucard isn't the perpetrator), an escalating antagonist, and a climax requiring forced cooperation. The binding moment — Alucard choosing to hold still while she pins his shadows — is the emotional core, showing his death-wish/trust hybrid and her earning the kill rather than being rescued. This satisfies "neither willing to show weakness first" and avoids the damsel trope the prompt warns against. Weaknesses: The villain (altar woman) is thin and functional, dispatched quickly. The word count falls short of the 1000-word seed (roughly 850). Some exchanges flirt with banality ("How observant." / "I know."). The ending, with its teasing openness, is slightly conventional for this genre of crossover fiction. The villagers are props. Alucard's line "I did" / "After I made it possible" is a nice touch of mutual acknowledgment, but the emotional resolution arrives somewhat easily given how brief their acquaintance is. Overall: competent, atmospheric, character-faithful work with excellent pacing and few flaws beyond minor thinness in the antagonist and slight under-length. Prison Strings Jolyne Cujoh & Makima Write a story where Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure) and Makima (Chainsaw Man) cross paths at a supernatural prison facility. Jolyne is immediately suspicious of Makima's falsely sweet demeanor, while Makima is intrigued by Jolyne's Stand ability. Their battle of wits escalates dangerously as Jolyne realizes how manipulative Makima truly is. **Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure)** Jolyne is the daughter of Jotaro Kujo and the first female JoJo protagonist. Her Stand, Stone Free, allows her to unravel her body into string that she can control. She's hot-headed, foul-mouthed, and doesn't take disrespect from anyone. She was framed for murder and sent to prison. She has a distinctive butterfly tattoo on her arm and wears her hair in two buns. Despite her tough exterior, she's deeply loyal to her friends and family. She can be impulsive but is highly adaptable in battle. She inherited her father's ability to stay cool under pressure but is more emotionally expressive. Famous quote: "If there's no Mickey, this shit ain't Disney!" **Makima (Chainsaw Man)** Makima appears as a young woman with auburn hair and ringed yellow eyes. She's the Control Devil who can dominate anyone she considers beneath her (nearly everyone). She maintains a pleasant, soft-spoken demeanor that masks her manipulative, cold nature. She can create contracts with humans and devils, often exploiting their desires. She's obsessed with Chainsaw Man and wants to control him. She keeps numerous people and devils as pets on leashes. She's practically immortal due to a contract with the Prime Minister. She views humans as lesser beings but mimics human emotions perfectly. Famous quote: "It's okay. Dogs are supposed to die for their owners." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
Chain-link fences within the yard rattle whenever an inmate passes by. At Green Dolphin Street Prison, that sound usually means someone is running from a guard. Today, nobody runs. The inmates drift toward the fence in a silent line, each holding a folded paper cup. Jolyne Cujoh watches from the laundry-room window. “What the hell is this?” A woman in a white visitor’s coat crosses the yard. Auburn hair, gentle smile, yellow eyes marked with concentric rings. She stops beside an inmate and takes his cup. He looks relieved, as though she has lifted something heavy from his hands. The woman looks up at Jolyne. Jolyne steps back before she can help it. An hour later, the woman enters the laundry room with two guards. Her visitor’s badge reads **MAKIMA — SPECIAL OVERSIGHT**. “Jolyne Cujoh,” she says. “I’ve heard you’re difficult.” “Depends who’s asking.” Makima’s smile warms. Nothing else about her does. “Someone who wants to help your friend.” The guards bring in Ermes. She is walking, but her face is blank. A bruise darkens one wrist. Jolyne’s hand tightens around a bedsheet. “Ermes?” Ermes turns her head. Her eyes find Jolyne’s, and for a second they are full of fear. Then she looks at Makima. Makima notices. Of course she does. “The annex has been doing experiments,” Makima says. “I can have her transferred somewhere safe. Both of you, if you cooperate.” “With what?” “I’d like to see what you can do with string.” Jolyne glances at the sheet in her fist. Beneath her sleeve, a fine strand of her own body winds around the laundry cart’s wheel. She hasn’t shown Makima a thing. “Sounds like somebody told you already.” “They told me you’re interesting.” Makima steps closer. “I’d rather decide for myself.” Jolyne sends the strand across the floor. It slips beneath Ermes’s shoe and curls around her ankle. Ermes flinches. Still herself in there. Makima looks down at precisely the right spot. “Careful,” she says softly. “You could hurt her.” Jolyne hates the way she makes it sound like concern. A buzzer shrieks. The guards seize Ermes and pull her through the door. Jolyne lunges, but Makima raises one finger. Across the room, a dryer caves inward with a deafening crash. Dust fills the air. By the time Jolyne can see, Ermes is gone. Makima remains in the doorway. “Come to the annex tonight,” she says. “Alone.” * The annex squats beyond the exercise yard, behind three locked gates. Officially, it houses inmates too dangerous for the ordinary blocks. Unofficially, Jolyne has seen its orderlies carry covered cages inside. She follows the strand still looped around Ermes’s ankle. It stretches thin through pipes, vents, and seams in the concrete. Stone Free lets her feel every tug. At midnight, it leads her to a room filled with people sitting in chairs. Guards. Inmates. An orderly Jolyne recognizes from the infirmary. Each holds a paper cup in both hands. Ermes sits in the center. Makima stands behind her, one hand resting lightly on her shoulder. “You came,” Makima says. “Your invitation sucked.” “I knew it would be enough.” Jolyne studies the room. Cameras in the corners. A sealed security door behind Makima. A maintenance grille overhead. Too many hostages to rush her. “What’s in the cups?” “Water.” “And what did you promise them?” Makima’s smile fades a fraction. “What they wanted to hear.” The orderly lifts his cup and drinks. At Makima’s quiet instruction, he puts it down again. His hand shakes so badly that water spills across his knees. Jolyne feels cold. “You don’t give a damn about helping anybody.” “I help people,” Makima says. “People are simply happier when they know what to do.” “Yeah? Tell Ermes to leave.” Makima strokes Ermes’s hair. “She can leave when you agree to work with me.” Jolyne pulls her strand free of Ermes’s ankle. It vanishes under the chairs. Makima watches her. “You’ve been laying threads since the laundry room.” “Then you know what happens if I pull.” “Several people could be injured.” That stops Jolyne. Not because Makima is bluffing. Because she isn’t. Makima comes around the chair. “You understand the choice. I’m asking very little of you.” Jolyne looks past her, toward the cameras. Makima has put Ermes where Jolyne will see her every second. She has filled the room with people Jolyne will be afraid to hurt. Even now, she is waiting for Jolyne to thank her for offering a way out. “Here’s my answer,” Jolyne says. “Fuck you.” Stone Free erupts from her arm. Makima raises her hand. The air cracks. A hole bursts through Jolyne’s shoulder, and she slams into the wall. Makima approaches as Jolyne slides down it. “That was impulsive.” “Runs in the family.” Jolyne spits blood. “So does planning ahead.” Her threads snap taut—not around the chairs, but above them. The maintenance grille tears loose. Inside it, dozens of lengths of string whip through the ventilation shaft to the security office. Jolyne has spent the walk in here feeding them through every gap she passes. The fire alarms go off. Sprinklers hammer the room. On the monitors, every annex door flashes red. Makima stops. “A fire drill?” “An evacuation.” Jolyne hauls herself upright. “The whole prison gets to see what’s in your basement.” She pulls again. The security door behind Makima rolls open. On the other side, guards and inmates are already stumbling into the corridor as the alarm releases their locks. For the first time, Makima looks away from Jolyne. Only for a moment. It is long enough. Stone Free catches Ermes by the waist and yanks her clear of the chair. Jolyne meets her at the door and shoves her into the crowd. “Go!” Ermes runs. Jolyne follows, shoulder burning, while Makima remains among the overturned chairs and abandoned cups. At the far end of the corridor, Jolyne glances back. Makima is watching her with that pleasant smile again. The alarm is still ringing; she makes no move to stop it. Jolyne turns the corner and catches up with Ermes. Whatever Makima plans next, she can plan it without them standing in front of her.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This crossover fic delivers a competent, tense cat-and-mouse encounter between Jolyne and Makima. The prose is lean and controlled, with short punchy sentences that suit both characters. Makima's menace is conveyed effectively through understatement—the paper cups, the blank-faced hostages, the quiet commands. Jolyne's voice is appropriately foul-mouthed and defiant ("Your invitation sucked," "Fuck you"), and her tactical use of Stone Free—pre-laying threads through the vents during the walk in—is a clever, believable JoJo-style gambit. Strengths: The show-don't-tell approach is strong throughout (Ermes's flinch, the orderly's shaking hand, Makima looking away "only for a moment"). The battle of wits escalates logically. The ending, with Makima simply watching them go with her pleasant smile intact, is chillingly in-character and avoids a false victory. Weaknesses: The piece is somewhat underdeveloped relative to its potential. Makima's power is used only once (the invisible force crushing the dryer/bursting Jolyne's shoulder) and her Control Devil nature is implied rather than explored—why can't she simply control Jolyne? This plot hole is never addressed. The stakes with Ermes resolve a bit too easily; Makima's passivity at the end feels like authorial convenience rather than fully earned characterization, though it can be read as Makima's long-game indifference. The middle section relies on some familiar beats (hostage room, "come alone" invitation), and the emotional complexity, while present, stays at a simmer rather than peaking. Some imagery is functional but not especially vivid. The piece hits its length target and instructions (third person, present tense) faithfully. Overall: a solid, professional piece of fan fiction with good tension and character voice, held back from excellence by a thin plot logic and a somewhat safe resolution. + Scp: Notes from the Future — Score: 84.5
Prompt:
Write an SCP report about a researcher who begins finding handwritten notes from their future self, warning about a containment breach that hasn't happened yet. The notes become increasingly desperate and incoherent, sometimes containing information that contradicts known reality. Include the Foundation's attempts to determine if this is an actual temporal anomaly or psychological manipulation by a contained entity, and the researcher's struggle to trust their own perception. First person (researcher's perspective with interspersed notes), past tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**SCP-7482 — Incident Report** **Author:** Dr. Mara Venn, Site-43 **Status:** Archived pending temporal and cognitohazard review I found the first note beneath my keyboard on Monday morning. It was written in my handwriting on the back of a requisition slip I had submitted the previous week. > **Do not authorize the pressure test on Thursday. At 02:17, Chamber Six will open. Tell Ibarra the lower seal is already cracked.** Chamber Six held SCP-4190, a contained entity capable of making personnel remember conversations that had not occurred. I had studied it for four years. I knew its methods, and I knew Ibarra had inspected the lower seal on Friday. His report showed no damage. I handed the note to Security without telling Ibarra what it said. I wanted his answer before he heard the warning. He examined the seal again and found it intact. By noon, Security had cleared my office camera footage. At 06:42, I had entered alone. The requisition slip was already beneath the keyboard when I arrived. The previous night’s footage showed an empty desk until a scheduled recording gap at 03:00. The gap lasted eleven seconds, as it did every night. The handwriting examiner found no hesitation, tracing, or sign of imitation. “You wrote it,” she told me. “I can’t tell you when.” The second note appeared inside my locked desk drawer on Tuesday. > **Ibarra will say the seal is intact. He is right until the pressure test. Cancel it anyway. Please don’t ask me what happened to him.** I cancelled the test. Operations reinstated it six hours later, citing an equipment deadline and the absence of evidence. By then, Ibarra had asked to be reassigned. He said I had watched him through the inspection window for nearly twenty minutes without responding when he spoke. I remembered being in my office at the time. My access log agreed with me. The ink results arrived that evening. Both notes contained traces of iridium, bismuth, and a fluorinated binder that matched none of the pens stocked or registered at Site-43. The paper was ordinary. The graphite smudge along one edge came from my desk pencil. We treated the notes as a possible temporal anomaly and a possible SCP-4190 exposure. Security isolated me from the chamber. A researcher who had never worked with the entity reviewed copies of the notes; another read only typed transcriptions. Both passed cognitive screening. Neither found a way to account for the physical notes. On Wednesday, the third note appeared in the pocket of a coat I had not worn since winter. > **The pressure test is a distraction. Check the fire door. There is no lower seal. I invented it because you wouldn’t listen to anything else.** I read that sentence until I could no longer picture the seal I had inspected dozens of times. I opened Chamber Six’s schematics. They showed a lower seal. So did Ibarra’s photographs. When I closed my eyes, I could remember drawing the seal into a diagram during my first month at the site. I could also remember being told, years later, that we had never built one. I asked Records for the original construction plans. The clerk showed me two signed copies. One included the seal; one did not. Their document numbers and approval dates were identical. That night, Foundation temporal specialists placed me under continuous observation. They numbered every sheet of paper in my quarters, collected my pens, and fitted the doors with independent mechanical seals. Psychology interviewed me twice. The first specialist asked whether I believed the notes came from the future. I said I believed someone wanted me to think they did. The next morning, a note was folded into my pillowcase. No seal had broken. The room camera showed me sleeping. > **You told them that. I told them that. It didn’t help. At 02:17, don’t let them open the fire door for Ibarra. He will sound like Ibarra.** The ink matched the earlier notes. Laboratory staff tested every available office pen again. They also sampled printer toner, maintenance markers, and the chamber’s pressure gauge fluid. None contained the binder. I requested a direct interview with SCP-4190. The request was denied. According to the denial, the entity had not vocalized or induced a false memory outside Chamber Six for eighty-three days. According to my notes from the previous month, I had interviewed it the week before. I found the audio file. It held fourteen minutes of ventilation noise and my voice asking questions. A second voice answered only once: “You should stop writing those.” I did not remember the interview. That frightened me more than the voice. I began checking each thought against a record before I trusted it, then checking who had made the record. I asked Ibarra to tell me where we had first met. He gave the answer I remembered. For an hour, that was enough. At 01:51 on Thursday, the final note appeared on my palm. I had been awake, seated between two observers. Neither had seen me touch a pen. > **no fire door no chamber no Ibarra** > **the breach is when you make them look** > **Mara if you can still read this leave your hand closed** There was ink beneath my fingernails. Analysis later found the same iridium, bismuth, and binder. At 02:16, an alarm reported a pressure loss in Chamber Six. The observers turned toward the monitor. I kept my hand closed. Onscreen, Ibarra stood outside the chamber’s fire door, striking it with both fists. I heard him through the intercom. He asked us to open it. His voice sounded exactly as it had when he reassured me about the seal. I told Security to leave the door shut. At 02:17, the pressure returned to normal. The camera showed an empty corridor. Security later established that Ibarra had been asleep in his quarters throughout the alarm. His door camera supported that account. The chamber instruments showed a pressure loss; the independent gauge showed none. No containment breach was recorded. I kept my hand closed until a medic asked to examine it. There was one more line on my palm, written beneath the others in letters so small I had missed them: > **Next time, ask why the alarm waited for you to read this.** I did not know whether the notes had prevented a breach, caused the alarm, or taught me to recognize an event that had never happened. I submitted this report before sleeping. I asked that no one show it to SCP-4190, and that someone tell me in the morning whether I had written it.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of SCP-format fiction that executes the prompt's requirements with discipline and craft. The first-person past-tense perspective is maintained throughout, the notes escalate in desperation and incoherence as requested, and the Foundation's dual-hypothesis investigation (temporal anomaly vs. SCP-4190 manipulation) is rendered through concrete procedural detail rather than exposition. The researcher's epistemic collapse—checking each thought against a record, then checking who made the record—is shown through action and is genuinely unsettling. The prose is spare and clinical in a way appropriate to the format, and this restraint amplifies the horror. Details like the iridium/bismuth ink analysis, the eleven-second recording gap, the two identical construction plans, and the audio file with fourteen minutes of ventilation noise are effective "show" moments that build dread without melodrama. The escalating contradictions (the seal exists/never existed; the interview happened/didn't) fulfill the "contradicts known reality" requirement elegantly. The climax—keeping the hand closed while "Ibarra" pounds on the fire door—is well-earned tension, and the final nested note ("ask why the alarm waited for you to read this") is a chilling, ambiguous ending that resists resolution. The closing line about asking whether she wrote the report is a strong final beat. Weaknesses: the piece is somewhat compressed relative to the 1000-word seed (it runs near that, which is fine), and some middle-section investigation beats could feel repetitive to readers less attuned to procedural detail. The Ibarra character remains thin, though this is arguably functional. The twist machinery (entity vs. time loop) is familiar territory in SCP fiction, though the execution is above average. Dialogue is minimal and functional; what exists is effective. The emotional register is controlled to the point of slight coldness—the researcher's fear is stated plainly once ("That frightened me more than the voice") rather than deeply explored, though this suits the clinical format. No purple prose, no overwrought moments, no unearned positivity—the ending is appropriately dark and unresolved. Coherence is high despite deliberate ambiguity; the ambiguity reads as intentional design, not confusion. + Scp: Unmarked Doors Archive — Score: 80.9
Prompt:
Write an SCP entry about a series of identical unmarked doors appearing in abandoned buildings worldwide that lead to a massive, architecturally impossible archive. Documents within reference a previous global civilization destroyed by an unspecified containment failure. Foundation researchers discover references to their own organization under a different name, including personnel files for current staff dated centuries ago. Include exploration logs revealing sections of the archive actively being removed by entities resembling hazmat teams who flee when approached, and evidence that O5 Council members have visited the archive without authorization. Third person (exploration team perspective) with recovered document excerpts. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Item #:** SCP-XXXX **Object Class:** Euclid **Special Containment Procedures:** Foundation property records and demolition permits are to be monitored for abandoned structures containing unmarked doors not present on prior floor plans. Confirmed structures are to be acquired or placed under the control of a cooperating agency. Entrances are to be concealed behind temporary walls. Demolition is prohibited. No document may be removed from SCP-XXXX without being photographed in situ and assigned a retrieval number. Personnel encountering individuals in protective suits inside SCP-XXXX are not to pursue them beyond the last surveyed junction. Access credentials recovered within SCP-XXXX are to be treated as compromised, regardless of their apparent age. **Description:** SCP-XXXX is an archive accessible through a series of doors in abandoned buildings worldwide. Forty-three doors have been confirmed in structures ranging from a vacant hospital in Poland to an unfinished shopping centre in Chile. All have the same dimensions, handle, hinge placement, and blank steel face. They bear no manufacturer’s marks. Several show substantially more corrosion than the buildings containing them; the door in the Chilean site, erected in 2009, has weathering consistent with prolonged exposure predating the structure. Opening any confirmed door reveals a room within SCP-XXXX. The rooms do not correspond to the space behind the doors. SCP-XXXX contains shelving halls, records offices, map repositories, loading bays, and stairwells whose observed arrangement cannot be reconciled into a single physical layout. A corridor measured at 1.8 kilometres on the outbound journey has been crossed in under four minutes on return. Windows overlooking interior courtyards have been found on walls whose opposite sides open into other rooms. Most holdings concern a global civilization for which no corroborating historical evidence has been located. Its administrative regions correspond approximately to present-day coastlines, but its infrastructure and population estimates do not. Records describe its destruction as the result of a “containment failure.” The nature of the contained subject is omitted from documents examined to date. The following material was recovered during initial surveys. > **PUBLIC RECOVERY BUREAU — DISTRIBUTION CIRCULAR 88-14** > Civil authorities must not describe the event as a natural disaster. This terminology has already delayed evacuation in seven jurisdictions. > > The containment failure remains unclassified by cause. Personnel are reminded that absence of a cause is not evidence of deliberate action. > > Archive copies of this circular are to be retained until civil government can be reconstituted. The circular’s attached distribution list named twenty-six agencies. One was the **Custodial Foundation**, whose stated duties included anomaly identification, suppression of public knowledge, and indefinite containment. Its insignia differed from that of the Foundation by a single additional bar. ### Exploration Log XXXX-7 **Team:** Survey Unit Theta-9, four personnel **Entry:** Former municipal records office, Osaka **Objective:** Locate the source of paper-removal sounds reported during Survey XXXX-5 At 09:12, Theta-9 entered a shelving hall designated H-31. Its east wall had been intact on the previous survey. It now contained a freight opening wide enough for two loaded trolleys. Beyond it, the team observed six figures wearing yellow protective suits and full-face respirators. They were transferring bound volumes from the shelves into grey wheeled containers. The figures’ suits had no visible insignia. Their containers were stencilled with inventory numbers in the same format used by the archive. They worked without speaking, removing entire shelf runs in numerical order. Behind them, H-31 continued into a section not recorded on Theta-9’s map. At 09:14, Technician Rao announced the team’s presence. All six figures stopped. One turned its respirator toward Rao, then closed the volume it was holding. The figures abandoned two containers and fled through the freight opening. Theta-9 followed as far as the threshold. Beyond it was a bare concrete landing and a stairwell descending out of sight. At 09:16, the team heard heavy doors closing at several levels below. They did not pursue. When Theta-9 returned to H-31, the freight opening had become a wall of shelving. The two abandoned containers remained on the surveyed side. Their contents concerned the Custodial Foundation’s personnel department. One recovered folder contained an employment file for Dr. Lena Voss, currently assigned to Site-43. It listed her correct birth date, education, and security clearance. Its appointment date was **17 September 1682**. The photograph was identical to the image taken for her Foundation identification badge in 2018, including a small tear in the photographic paper that does not appear on the digital original. Twenty-one further files identified current Foundation employees. Dates ranged from 1641 to 1896. In thirteen cases, the files recorded assignments at sites that do not exist in Foundation records. Four contained performance reviews signed by supervisors who are currently employed, all of whom deny writing them. Dr. Voss was not informed of the file until its contents had been independently verified. She reported no memory of the Custodial Foundation. A handwriting comparison found that signatures attributed to her in six documents matched samples she provided under observation. ### Exploration Log XXXX-11 Theta-9 returned to H-31 equipped with a tethered camera system. The shelving wall was still present. At 11:28, the team found a second cleared section two halls north: a rectangular space where shelving, floor tiles, and ceiling fixtures had been removed. Fresh scrape marks led to a service lift. Inside the lift was a paper manifest, torn from a pad. Its upper half listed thirty-one containers and the instruction **WITHDRAW BEFORE TRANSFER**. Below the list were five signatures. Three matched signatures held in O5 Council access records. The manifest bore the previous day’s date. Security review found no authorized Council visit to any SCP-XXXX entrance on that date. Subsequent review identified footage from two monitored doors showing persons matching O5-2 and O5-7 entering alone on separate occasions. In each recording, the relevant door had been sealed behind a temporary wall before the visitor arrived. Neither wall showed evidence of forced entry. Both visitors emerged carrying empty document cases. When questioned, the Council issued a joint statement that no visit had been authorized. Individual members declined to confirm or deny their presence in the footage. The latest recovered container contained a partial index headed **FOUNDATIONS ESTABLISHED AFTER FAILURE**. The current Foundation’s name appears on the list. Its entry gives no establishment date. In the column labelled *Disposition*, a handwritten notation reads: > Not yet notified. Leave the doors where they will find them.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong, disciplined SCP entry that hits every required element: identical unmarked doors in abandoned buildings worldwide, an architecturally impossible archive, references to a prior global civilization destroyed by a containment failure, the Foundation's predecessor ("Custodial Foundation"), personnel files for current staff dated centuries ago, hazmat-suited entities removing documents who flee when approached, and evidence of unauthorized O5 visits. The prompt's formal constraints (third person, exploration logs, recovered document excerpts) are followed precisely, and the ~1000 word target is respected. The prose is clinical and controlled, well-suited to the SCP format. The strongest moments are concrete and specific: the photograph with the tear that "does not appear on the digital original," the manifest dated the previous day, the final handwritten notation "Not yet notified. Leave the doors where they will find them." That closing line is an excellent, understated twist that reframes the doors as deliberate bait and implies the Foundation is being managed — a genuinely unsettling implication delivered without melodrama. The hazmat entity scene is handled with restraint: the figure turning its respirator toward Rao, closing the volume, and fleeing is more effective than any elaborate description would be. The architectural impossibility is conveyed through concrete measurements (the 1.8 km corridor, windows on walls with rooms behind them) rather than vague assertion — good show-don't-show craft. Weaknesses: the piece is efficient to a fault; it can feel like a checklist of revelations delivered in sequence, with little breathing room. Characters are functional rather than nuanced — Dr. Voss is a plot device, and Theta-9 personnel are names only. This is largely inherent to the SCP format, but the best entries give researchers a bit more texture. The middle section (personnel files) slightly rushes through what could be the most emotionally resonant material. Dialogue is minimal and purely functional. The O5 section resolves a touch too neatly — the footage evidence arrives conveniently. Still, the piece is coherent, tonally consistent, and its implications accumulate effectively. The ending earns its darkness through established logic rather than shock. + Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Le Guin) — Score: 85.2
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Author style: Le Guin) Write a chapter following a young diplomatic envoy sent to address tensions on a distant human colony where humanity has diverged into distinct subspecies through both natural adaptation and separation of lineages. Against protocol, the envoy slips away from official functions to walk the streets alone, encountering markets, ordinary citizens, and social structures that contradict the official briefings. Upon returning to their quarters, the envoy is reprimanded by Command, and is tasked with approaching the stationed Minister of Science (a political posting rather than scientific). A challenging conversation ensues, in which the envoy's wits and will are tested, by a seasoned political operator looking to test the mettle of the offworlder. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The first thing Sera noticed about the city was that nobody wore a cloak. On the landing platform, the reception party had been clothed in the manner prescribed by the mission brief: pale wraps, bare arms, bare feet. Sera had taken them for ceremonial dress. But the porters in the street wore no more, nor did the tram drivers, nor the children darting between the wheels of handcarts. Cloth here covered what needed covering. Everything else belonged to the air. Her cloak, a dark green diplomatic garment with a clasp at the throat, drew eyes all the way down the hill. She had been told not to leave the Residence without an escort. The order had come after six hours of welcome speeches about kinship, cooperation, and the enduring unity of humankind. Sera had waited until the last official vehicle departed, then gone out through the kitchen yard. At the market, a man selling small silver fish called to her in Trade Speech. “You’re losing water, offworlder.” “I haven’t spilled any.” “Under all that.” He pointed at her cloak. “You’ll be thirsty before you’re hungry.” His skin was dark and smooth, except for the ridges along his neck that opened and closed as he spoke. Sera knew the ridges from the brief. The Tideborn had lived in the estuary settlements for almost nine hundred years, first by choice and then because the inland aquifers failed. Their children were not always Tideborn; lineages crossed, and bodies did not observe the neat divisions of the colonial census. Still, the brief had described them as *confined largely to littoral labor*. “What do you do with the fish you don’t sell?” she asked. “Eat them.” He grinned. “Some things are simple.” Beside him sat an inland woman, compact and broad-chested, her nostrils pinched nearly shut against the damp air. She was mending a net with swift, blunt fingers. On the board behind them, prices were written in three scripts. Sera bought a paper cone of salted fish. The woman named a price; the man corrected it downward. “You’ll ruin me,” the woman said. “She’s a guest.” “She’s a diplomat.” “So she can afford to be a guest.” Sera paid the first price. The woman watched her put away the change. “Have they told you we can’t agree on anything?” she asked. “They’ve told me there are disputes over water rights.” “There are.” She knotted a loop of net. “My sister thinks I drink too much tea, too.” Farther on, the market opened beneath a canopy of woven reeds. Sera saw people she could not place in any of the brief’s categories: a tall young man with the fine, reflective eyelids of the upland families carrying a Tideborn child on his shoulders; two women, one heavy-boned and one slight, arguing over the construction of a communal cistern; a registrar at a folding desk taking names from anyone who approached. The official charts had shown three populations occupying three territories. The city had lanes, courtyards, and households. At the registrar’s table, an elderly man waited while a girl read a form aloud to him. His hands trembled too badly to hold it. The girl wore a cord around her upper arm with three colored knots. “What does that mean?” Sera asked when the old man had gone. “It means I can witness for three wards,” the girl said. “What does your cloak mean?” Sera looked down at the clasp bearing the seal of the Mission. “It means I’m permitted to speak for people who aren’t here.” The girl considered this. “That must be difficult.” Sera walked back before sunset. On the way, she passed a row of public taps. Each tap bore the name of a ward, and each had a different queue. People stepped from one queue to another to hold a place for a neighbor or pass along a vessel. At the last tap, two men were shouting while a third tried to repair the handle between them. The disputes were real. So, plainly, was the life around them. Command was waiting in her quarters. He did not rise when she entered. His uniform coat lay folded beside him; even indoors he seemed dressed for inspection. “You were seen,” he said. “I thought I might be.” “You went out alone.” “Yes.” “After an explicit instruction.” “Yes.” He shut his eyes briefly. “Envoy Sera, the Minister has people who would make excellent use of an incident involving you. A complaint from a vendor. A misunderstanding at a checkpoint. You don’t know the ground here.” “No,” she said. “I know a little more of it than I did this morning.” Command studied her damp cloak. “Then you can put it to use. Minister Vey has requested a private conversation tomorrow. I’d intended to send you after you’d read the remainder of the files.” “What does he want?” “To find out whether you believe what’s in them. And whether you’ll say so.” The Minister of Science received her in a room without instruments. There were old maps on the walls and a basin of cool water between the chairs. Vey was a small man with an uplander’s narrow hands. He poured a cup for himself but did not offer one to her. “I hear you visited our market,” he said. “Does everybody?” “By tomorrow.” He sipped. “Your Command is displeased.” “He told me.” “Yet you came here on his errand.” Vey set down his cup. “Tell me what you saw.” Sera had prepared an answer on the walk over. She let it go. “People buying food,” she said. “People working. A broken tap.” “An attentive traveler could see as much from a tram.” His expression remained pleasant. “What did you see that your people did not expect?” “A registrar authorized by three wards. Shared work between lineages. A price agreed for my benefit by two people who didn’t agree about the price.” “And from these charming sights you conclude there is no conflict.” “I didn’t say that.” “No. Your predecessors generally did.” Sera looked at the maps. They divided the colony into clean bands of blue, ocher, and white. At the edges of each band, towns had been marked with small black dots. “The brief calls the wards segregated,” she said. “But it gives only their boundaries. I don’t know who drew them, or when.” Vey leaned back. “The boundaries are necessary. Different bodies need different water, shelter, and air.” “Sometimes. Do the queues at the taps follow those needs?” “People follow habit as faithfully as need.” “Then I need to learn which is which.” For the first time, he offered her water. Sera took it. The cup was cool enough to hold against her forehead. “You are young,” Vey said. “That is usually an advantage to the people who send you. They can tell you what you’ve learned.” “And what would you tell them?” “That the colony is peaceful, if you ask me here. In Council tomorrow, I will tell them we are on the edge of a crisis.” He folded his hands. “Both statements have served me. Which one would you report?” Sera thought of the man bracing the broken tap while his neighbors shouted past him. A report could make him proof of concord or proof of collapse. Either way, the handle would still be broken. “I’d report that you said both,” she answered. “Then I’d ask to see the water accounts.” Vey laughed once, without warmth or contempt. “Good,” he said. “Now we can begin.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a disciplined, quietly accomplished piece that captures Le Guin's anthropological register with real fidelity. The opening image—the cloak as cultural marker—establishes theme through concrete detail rather than exposition, and the market sequence does exactly what the prompt asks: it contradicts the official brief through observed life (the registrar's three knots, the shared queues at the taps, the vendor correcting a price downward). The dialogue is the strongest element; it is oblique, subtextual, and character-revealing, particularly the exchange with the girl at the registrar's table ("It means I'm permitted to speak for people who aren't here" / "That must be difficult"), which lands as genuine Le Guin-style irony. The Command reprimand is efficient and believable, though Command himself remains a sketch. The Vey conversation is the centerpiece and mostly earns its weight: the withheld water, the maps, the admission that he tells different truths in different rooms. Sera's final answer—reporting both statements and asking for the water accounts—is a satisfying display of wit that doesn't strain plausibility. The closing "Now we can begin" is a touch conventional, the most genre-expected beat in the piece. Weaknesses: the subspecies worldbuilding, while handled with restraint, is fairly standard adaptive-divergence material (gill ridges, pinched nostrils, reflective eyelids). The broken tap as a unifying symbol is slightly neat—Sera's reflection on it ("Either way, the handle would still be broken") borders on the aphoristic. Some minor characters blur together. The prose is clean and controlled but rarely transcendent; it imitates Le Guin's plainness without always achieving her resonance. Length is close to the 1000-word seed. No purple prose, no meandering, no tonal lapses; the piece is coherent, understated, and emotionally restrained by design—which limits its emotional range even as it suits the mode. + Biopunk: Polymerase Chain Reaction — Score: 78.7
Prompt:
Biopunk -- Polymerase Chain Reaction Write a chapter set in a near-future post-apocalyptic world where corporate genetic engineering was designed with built-in obsolescence—engineered DNA lasting only one generation to maximize profits before societal collapse. Follow a biohacker working with salvaged equipment to splice viable food crops for their settlement using rapidly degrading genetic material. As world building / window dressing, include details about jury-rigged lab equipment, and the physical toll (and unexpected upsides) of using untested genetic modifications as medicine. The plot of this chapter is centred around a black market contract. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Polymerase Chain Reaction The contract arrived in a jar of honey. Mara held it to the lamp. Beneath the amber syrup floated a strip of black plastic, rolled tight enough to fit through the jar’s neck. On it, in white type, were three lines: **TWELVE VIABLE BRASSICA LINES.** **DELIVERY BEFORE FIRST FROST.** **PAYMENT: ONE UNLICENSED MATERNAL SEED LOT.** She read the last line twice. Outside the greenhouse, Settlement Nine’s children were stripping yellow leaves from the final stand of winter cabbage. Their parents had saved seed from last year’s crop, as their parents had done before the corporate farms. Half of it had failed to sprout. The rest had grown leaves too thin to survive a cold snap. One harvest. That was what the companies had sold, right up to the collapse. Corn that fed a town brilliantly and left sterile kernels. Rice that grew in salt water until its offspring lost the trait. The contracts called it *licensed continuity*. Mara called it hunger with paperwork. She opened the jar. The honey smelled real. Her lab occupied the shell of an old bus. Bicycle chains drove a salvaged centrifuge. A refrigerator compressor cooled the storage box; when the electricity failed, wet cloth and night air did what they could. The thermal cycler had once belonged to a veterinary clinic. Its display was dead, so Mara judged its moods by the clicking relay and the cheap thermometer wired through the lid. Across the workbench stood six empty canisters from Helixor, the biotech giant that had patented most of the region’s food. Their labels still promised *a better tomorrow, every season*. Mara had scrubbed them clean and filled them with the few reagents she had left. Every time she reached for one, Helixor’s bright green logo flashed under her hand. She unrolled the plastic strip. The broker’s mark was punched into one corner: a tiny square hole inside a larger one. Pell. He had bought medicines for Settlement Nine before, and sold them at a profit to someone else. A second strip lay inside the first. **CLIENT PROVIDES SOURCE MATERIAL. NO QUESTIONS.** By dusk, a stranger brought a packet of seeds wrapped in three layers of oilcloth. She wore a patched raincoat and carried a pistol with no magazine. “Where did Pell get these?” Mara asked. “He didn’t,” the stranger said. “I did.” Mara tipped a few seeds into her palm. Brassica, by their shape. Dark, sound, and impossibly old if the handwriting on the packet was genuine. **MOTHER STOCK. DO NOT DISTRIBUTE.** The stranger watched her read it. “Can you do the job?” “Growing them takes longer than the time you’ve given me.” “I know.” “Then what does Pell expect me to deliver?” “Twelve lines your people can plant after frost. Seed from these, not just leaves.” Mara closed her hand around the seeds. “Who are you?” “Someone who took them out of a Helixor vault.” That night Mara ran fragments from the packet through the battered cycler. The machine clicked and steamed. She slept beside it with her coat over her knees, waking whenever it fell silent. In the morning, the results were faint but legible. The old seed carried pieces of the traits Helixor had leased to farms across the continent: cold tolerance, fast growth, resistance to the blight that still stained the greenhouse glass. Some fragments had broken down in storage. Others were intact. And beside them was a sequence Mara had seen in every commercial crop she’d tested. It did no harm to the parent plant. In the next generation, it ruined the seed. She ran the test again. The stranger waited outside, sitting on the bus steps with her empty pistol across her lap. “You knew,” Mara said when she came out. “I hoped I was wrong.” “Your mother stock is Helixor stock.” The stranger’s face changed, though only a little. “The vault inventory said it predated the lock.” “The packet might. These seeds don’t.” Mara sat beside her. “Pell’s offering to pay me with another lot like this?” “He has one that grows true. I saw it.” “Then why does he need twelve more?” “He’s selling them east. One seed lot won’t feed all his buyers.” Mara looked toward the greenhouse. The children had piled the stripped leaves into baskets. Even the yellow ones would go into soup. Three winters earlier, Mara had dosed herself with an untested repair treatment after a glass shard pierced her lung. It had closed the wound. It had also left a web of hard tissue along her ribs that tightened whenever the air turned cold. She pressed a hand there now and felt the familiar catch as she breathed in. The treatment had changed her in one useful way. She could smell mold before it showed on a dish, a sour-metal note so sharp she could pick a contaminated tray out of a row. She had saved whole planting beds that way. She still would have preferred an ordinary lung. “There’s no time to make twelve lines,” she told the stranger. “Not safely. I can start them. I can find out which plants might hold their traits in the next seed. That’s what he gets before frost.” “He’ll say you broke the contract.” “Pell knew what he was asking. Let him explain how twelve harvest-tested lines were supposed to appear in six weeks.” The stranger stood. “And the seed lot?” “We take payment first.” At noon, Pell came in person, riding a motorbike that burned cooking oil. He left it idling outside the bus. Mara showed him twelve labeled trays beneath the grow lamps, each holding a cluster of new green leaves. He barely glanced at them. “Where are the seeds?” “Not grown yet.” “Then the contract isn’t filled.” “The contract says viable lines. They’re alive. If you meant proven seed, you should have brought me the source last spring.” Pell smiled without warmth. “I can take my packet back.” Mara opened one of the Helixor canisters and set it on the bench between them. Inside lay the tested samples, sealed and labeled. “You can. But your eastern buyers will want to know why their harvests fail the following year.” He stared at the canister. “You tested them.” “Twice.” For a long moment, the only sound was the refrigerator compressor rattling under the bench. Pell reached into his coat and brought out a small tin. He put it beside the canister. “The payment lot. Test it too.” “I will.” “And if it’s good?” Mara looked past him at the children carrying their baskets home. “You can have cuttings from the twelve plants when they’re strong enough. Settlement Nine keeps the plants and whatever seed they make. Any buyer of yours gets told what the tests found.” “That wasn’t our deal.” “No,” Mara said. “It’s the one I can keep.” Pell took his hand off the tin. Outside, his motorbike sputtered and died. By evening, Mara had opened the payment lot. The seeds inside were small and pale, with no company stamp on the paper around them. She put the first few in a damp tray and carried the rest to cold storage. They would have to grow before she could trust them. She knew that now better than anyone. In the greenhouse, someone had set a bowl of cabbage soup by her stool. Mara ate while she watched the twelve trays under their lamps. Beyond the glass, frost silvered the empty fields.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a disciplined, well-structured chapter that hits nearly all prompt requirements: the biopunk post-apocalyptic setting, built-in genetic obsolescence ("licensed continuity"), jury-rigged lab equipment (bus lab, bicycle-chain centrifuge, dead-display thermal cycler), the physical toll and unexpected upside of untested gene treatment (hardened rib tissue vs. mold-sensing smell), and a black market contract as the plot's spine. The honey-jar contract delivery is a strong, economical opening hook. Strengths: The prose is lean and controlled, with a consistent dry, pragmatic voice well matched to Mara. World-building is delivered through concrete objects (Helixor canisters, the punched broker's mark, the empty pistol) rather than exposition dumps. The twist—that the "mother stock" carries the obsolescence gene—is well set up and thematically resonant. The confrontation with Pell resolves through leverage and testing rather than violence, which feels earned and in character. The ending's conditional hope ("They would have to grow before she could trust them") suits the world. Weaknesses: The stranger is underdeveloped, functioning mostly as a plot device; her motivations remain thin. Some dialogue is functional rather than alive ("Can you do the job?" / "I know"). The plot beats—mysterious client, hidden test, confrontation with broker—are somewhat predictable in outline, though executed cleanly. The emotional register stays even throughout; there's little variation in tension, and the children/soup imagery, while effective once, is leaned on twice. Pell is a stock antagonist. The word count is roughly on target. Nothing is purple or overwrought; the restraint is a virtue, though it occasionally tips into flatness.
